Bienvenue!

Welcome — how to use this guide

You can teach this — even if you don't speak French

This guide is built for a family where the child is learning French and the parent is not (yet!). You do not need to be fluent. You need to be curious, consistent and brave — which is exactly what you want your child to be. Three tools make it possible:

  • Every French word has a speaker button. Tap it and your device reads the French aloud. Use Voice: Slow · Lent in the header when you or your child need to hear it more slowly.
  • Every French word has an English translation and a pronunciation hint written in English sounds, e.g. Bonjourbo(n)-ZHOORHello. The hint gets you close; the speaker button gets you right.
  • Every lesson has a Parent Teaching Guide with exact words to say, the mistakes to expect, and signs that your child has truly understood.
Checking for a French voice on this device…
Set up the voice firstTest the voice now: tap Bonjour! Je suis prêt. On commence?bo(n)-ZHOOR, zhuh swee preh. o(n) ko-MA(N)SSHello! I'm ready. Shall we begin?. If you hear English-accented French or nothing at all, add a French voice: on iPhone/iPad go to Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices → French (choose Canada if offered); on Windows go to Settings → Time & Language → Speech → Add voices → Français (Canada); on Android go to Settings → Text-to-speech → install French. Then reload this page.
How the guide is organised

The Ontario French Immersion curriculum for Grade 1 has four strands, one per tab: A. Écouter (Listening), B. Parler (Speaking), C. Lire (Reading) and D. Écrire (Writing). Each strand has 9 lessons, a word wall and a progress tracker. The lessons are matched to 9 monthly themes, so in any given month all four strands talk about the same topic — the words your child hears in the Listening lesson come back in Speaking, then Reading, then Writing. That repetition is how children build a language.

Every lesson follows the same nine steps: Wonder Hook → Objectives → Parent Guide → The Lesson → Think Like a Linguist → Classwork → Assignment → Homework → Keep Wondering. Each lesson is meant to fill one full week of short daily sessions, not one sitting.

The golden rules of teaching French at home
  1. Little and often beats long and rare. 20 minutes of French every day is worth far more than two hours on Saturday.
  2. French for routines, English for explanations. Use French every time you do something repeatable (greetings, the calendar, “sit down”, “well done”). Use English freely to explain ideas — this is how Grade 1 immersion teachers work too, except they mime instead of translating.
  3. Gestures, pictures and objects first; translation last. When you introduce a new word, point, act, draw or hold the object. Show the English only if your child is stuck.
  4. Mistakes are the lesson. Never say “No, wrong.” Repeat the sentence back correctly with a smile (“Ah, j'ai six ans! Super!”). This is called recasting and it works better than correcting.
  5. Be a learner in front of your child. Say “I don't know that word — let's find out together.” Children who watch a parent learn become fearless learners.
  6. Listening comes before speaking. Many children understand for weeks before they speak. That silent period is normal; keep talking to them in French.
Materials for the whole year
  • A dedicated notebook called Mon cahier de français (a lined primary notebook with a picture space at the top is ideal) and a second one for the Mon dictionnaire word book (Unit 2).
  • Pencils, eraser, crayons or markers, glue stick, scissors, index cards, sticky notes, a few folders.
  • A wall space or large paper for a mur de mots (word wall) — you will add words all year.
  • A soft toy or puppet that “only speaks French”. Many immersion teachers use one; children will speak French to a puppet long before they will to an adult.
  • Library card: Ontario public libraries have French picture books and audiobooks. Ask the librarian for “French first readers” and “albums en français”.
Why this mattersFrench is an official language of Canada and is spoken by more than 300 million people on five continents. In Ontario alone, over 600,000 people speak French as their first language — more than in any other province except Quebec.

Le plan de l'année

The year plan, week by week

Thirty-six lessons plus three review weeks = 39 school weeks, the length of an Ontario school year. Each unit is taught in the order Listen → Speak → Read → Write, because that is the natural order in which children acquire a language: they hear it, then say it, then recognise it in print, then produce it. Click any lesson to jump to it.

PacingBehind schedule? Totally fine. Holidays, illness and busy weeks happen. Never skip the Listening and Speaking lessons of a unit; if you must compress, shorten the Assignment. Ahead of schedule? Don't rush to the next lesson — do the Keep Wondering questions as mini-projects, read extra French books, and replay the audio texts.

What “done” looks like at the end of Grade 1

By June, a child who has worked through this guide should be able to: follow everyday instructions given in French; greet people correctly (and know when to say tu or vous); introduce themselves and their family; name colours, numbers to 31, body parts, clothes, foods, animals, days and months; read short patterned books aloud; write simple sentences such as J'aime les pommes. or Aujourd'hui, il fait froid.; and talk about French-speaking communities in Ontario and around the world.

Les sons du français

The sounds of French — a pronunciation primer for parents

French has about 36 sounds, and a handful don't exist in English. You don't need to master them before teaching — you'll improve alongside your child. Play each example, copy it, then have your child copy you. Treat it like a game of echoes.

How to read the pronunciation hints in this guide
  • CAPITALS show the syllable to lean on. In French it is almost always the last syllable: ba-TOH, not BA-toh.
  • (n) means a nasal sound: push the vowel through your nose and do not close your mouth to say the n. bo(n)-ZHOOR, not bon-joor.
  • zh is the sound in the middle of “measure”.
  • ü or “(rounded)” means: say “ee” but round your lips as if to whistle.
  • The hints are approximate. Always trust the speaker button over the spelling.

Four rules that unlock most French words
  1. Final consonants are usually silent. petitpuh-TEEsmall, chatshacat, vousvooyou (formal/plural). Memory trick: consonants in the word CaReFuL (c, r, f, l) are often pronounced at the end: sacsakbag, mermehrsea, neufnuhfnine, animala-nee-MALanimal.
  2. A final -e is silent but makes the consonant before it heard: vertvehrgreen (masc.) vs vertevehrtgreen (fem.).
  3. Liaison: a silent final consonant wakes up when the next word starts with a vowel: les amislay-za-MEEthe friends, un éléphantuh(n)-nay-lay-FA(N)an elephant.
  4. Accents change sounds: é = “ay”, è/ê = “eh”. The accent on à and où only tells words apart; it doesn't change the sound.
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?The letter h is silent in every French word — but some words beginning with h act as if the h were a consonant, so there's no liaison. French speakers call it the h aspiré. le hibouluh ee-BOOthe owl is one of them. Even adults learning French trip on this — you now know something many high-school graduates don't.

Good to knowMum or dad? Some French words change with the speaker. A mother says Je suis fière; a father says Je suis fier (the sound is identical — only the spelling changes). When you praise a girl, Tu es prête? (Are you ready?); a boy, Tu es prêt?

Le rituel du matin

The daily morning routine

Every Grade 1 immersion classroom starts the day with the same short routine. Its magic is repetition: after a month, your child will say it on their own. Do it every school day, in French, in the same order, standing by a wall calendar. 5–10 minutes.

Build it gradually
UnitAdd to the routine
1 (Sept)Greeting + Comment ça va? only.
2 (Oct)Add counting the days of school so far (1, 2, 3… — a straw or tally for each day). Count in French.
3 (Nov)Add Quel jour sommes-nous? (days of the week song).
5 (Jan)Add Qu'est-ce qu'on porte? (clothing).
8 (Apr)Add the full date and the weather — the complete routine above.

Les jours de la semaine · Days of the week

lundiluh(n)-DEEMondaymardimar-DEETuesdaymercredimehr-kruh-DEEWednesdayjeudizhuh-DEEThursdayvendrediva(n)-druh-DEEFridaysamedisam-DEESaturdaydimanchedee-MA(N)SHSunday
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?French days of the week don't start with capital letters — and neither do months. lundi comes from Lune (Moon), mardi from Mars, mercredi from Mercury, jeudi from Jupiter and vendredi from Venus. The week is a little solar system!

Ressources et évaluation

Resources, assessment and your data

Free French for young children
  • Groupe Média TFO — Ontario's own French-language public broadcaster, with a children's section (Mini TFO) full of songs, cartoons and games made for Franco-Ontarian kids: tfo.org.
  • Radio-Canada — Canada's French public broadcaster; its youth section has cartoons and stories: ici.radio-canada.ca.
  • Your public library — French picture books (albums), easy readers and audiobooks. Many libraries also lend French e-books through their apps.
  • Franco-Ontarian events near you — Franco-Ontarian Day (September 25), winter carnivals, cabane à sucre outings in March and Saint-Jean-Baptiste celebrations on June 24. Search your city name + “francophone”.
  • Your local French-language school board or ACFO (Assemblée de la francophonie de l'Ontario) regional office often posts family events that are free and welcoming to learners.
How to assess your child (like a teacher would)

Ontario teachers grade Grade 1 French on four levels. Use the same idea at the end of each unit, for each strand, and write the level in the back of the notebook.

LevelWhat it looks likeIn plain words
1Understands/uses a few words with lots of help, gestures and EnglishBeginning
2Understands/uses familiar words and short phrases with some helpDeveloping
3Understands/uses the unit's words and sentence patterns with little help — this is the provincial standardGot it
4Uses the language flexibly, adds new words, helps othersBeyond

Keep a portfolio: one folder per unit containing the best Assignment, a photo of the Classwork, and a short audio or video of your child speaking (use your phone). In June, watch the September video together. Nothing motivates a child more than hearing how far they've come.

Where the content comes from

Every lesson is tagged with the expectation codes from The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 1–8: French as a Second Language — Core, Extended, and French Immersion (2013), French Immersion Grade 1: Strand A (Listening), B (Speaking), C (Reading), D (Writing). All 39 specific expectations are covered, most of them several times. The official text is on the Ministry's Curriculum and Resources site: dcp.edu.gov.on.ca.

Your data

Everything you type in the boxes and every progress tick saves automatically in this browser on this device. It isn't sent anywhere. If you switch devices or clear your browser data, it won't come with you — so keep the paper notebook as your real record.

Strand A · Listening

Écouter

Listening is where every language begins. In Grade 1 immersion, children learn to understand far more than they can say: they follow instructions, enjoy songs and stories, catch the main idea without knowing every word, and learn how French speakers greet each other. Each lesson builds a listening strategy your child will use for life. All 9 listening expectations (A1.1–A3.2) are covered.
Strand progress0%

Lessons · Leçons

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 1 · Unit 1 · Bonjour!

Bonjour! J'écoute les salutations

Hello! Listening for greetings

A1.1A1.2A3.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

In English, you might say “Hey!” to your best friend but “Good morning” to your principal. French speakers do the same thing — but they go even further: they have two different words for “you”, one for friends and one for grown-ups they respect.

Here's the puzzle: if you walked into a French school tomorrow and nobody explained anything, how could you figure out which greeting to use with whom — just by listening and watching? What clues would you look for?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A1.1Use three listening strategies — look for clues, listen for words I know, ask when I don't understand — before, during and after listening.
  • A1.2Explain why I am listening: to enjoy a song, to hear new French sounds, or to know how to greet someone.
  • A3.2Recognise friendly greetings (Salut!) and polite greetings (Bonjour, Madame) and when each one is used.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Before you begin (15 minutes, alone)

Play every speaker button in The Lesson below. Say each phrase out loud three times. Don't worry about sounding perfect; your child needs to see you try. Then print or draw two simple cards: one with a waving hand (Bonjour – hello) and one with a hand waving goodbye (Au revoir – goodbye).

How to introduce the topic (Monday)
  1. Stand at the door of the room and greet your child in French as if they are arriving at school: Bonjour, mon ami! / Bonjour, mon amie!bo(n)-ZHOOR, mo(n) na-MEEHello, my friend! (boy / girl) Shake hands, smile, wave. Say nothing in English.
  2. Ask the Wonder Hook question in English. Let your child guess. Do not give the answer. Write their ideas on a sticky note — you'll come back to them on Friday.
  3. Read The Lesson together. You read the English story; tap the speakers for the French. Pause after each French phrase and have your child echo it.
You can say“Today we are going to be language detectives. Detectives don't know everything at the start — they collect clues. When you hear French, your clues are: people's faces, their hands, the place they're in, and any words you already know.”
Key teaching moments
  • The three listening strategies are the heart of this lesson and will be used all year. Name them every time: Before — look at pictures and guess. During — listen for words you know. After — ask a question. Make a small poster with three icons: an eye, an ear, a question mark.
  • Salut vs Bonjour. Salut is casual (friends, siblings, kids). Bonjour is always safe and polite — with anyone. Rule of thumb for your child: “When in doubt, say Bonjour.”
  • Madame and Monsieur. In French it is polite to add them after Bonjour when greeting an adult: Bonjour, Madame. Children in French schools call their teacher Madame or Monsieur (sometimes followed by the teacher's first name).
Watch for this misconceptionChildren often think Bonjour only means “good morning” because jour means day. In fact Bonjour works all day long, from morning until evening. In the evening, people switch to Bonsoir (good evening).
Watch for this misconceptionYour child may think French is “just English with different words”. Gently show that French has rules English doesn't, like the polite vous. This is exciting, not scary: it's a new way of thinking!
How you'll know it clickedYour child can hear a French greeting (played from the speaker or said by you) and correctly show whether the person is saying hello or goodbye, and whether they're talking to a friend or an adult. They can also name at least one listening strategy in their own words (“I looked at the picture first”).

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Léa's first day

Meet Léa. She is six years old and lives in Sudbury, Ontario, a city where lots of people speak French. Today is her first day of Grade 1 at a French school. She's a little nervous. Her tummy feels like it has butterflies in it.

When Léa walks into the classroom, her teacher smiles and says: Bonjour, Léa!bo(n)-ZHOOR, lay-AHello, Léa! Léa smiles back and says: Bonjour, Madame!bo(n)-ZHOOR, ma-DAMHello, Ma'am! (to a female teacher)

Then Léa sees her friend Noah from the park. Noah waves and shouts: Salut, Léa!sa-LÜ, lay-AHi, Léa! Léa laughs and says: Salut, Noah!sa-LÜ, no-AHi, Noah!

Did you notice? Léa used two different words for hello! She said Bonjour to her teacher and Salut to her friend. Why do you think she did that?

Part 2 · Hello words and goodbye words

French has special words for when you arrive and special words for when you leave. Listen to each one. Wave your hand toward yourself for hello words and wave goodbye for goodbye words.

Les salutations · Greetings

Bonjourbo(n)-ZHOORHello (to anyone, all day)Salutsa-LÜHi / Bye (to friends)Bonsoirbo(n)-SWARGood eveningAu revoiroh ruh-VWARGoodbyeÀ demaina duh-MA(N)See you tomorrowBonne journéebunn zhoor-NAYHave a good dayBonne nuitbunn NWEEGood nightÀ bientôta byah(n)-TOHSee you soon

Here is a detective secret: Salut is a magic word. It can mean hi and bye, but only with friends! You have to listen to when someone says it. If they're arriving, it means hi. If they're leaving, it means bye.

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Bonjour is made of two little words: bon (good) + jour (day). So every time you say bonjour, you're really saying “good day”! And bonsoir is bon + soir (evening).
Part 3 · How ARE you?

After hello, French speakers often ask how you are. The question is short: Comment ça va?ko-MA(N) sa VAHow are you? / How's it going? Here are three answers. Make the face that matches each one!

Ça va bien!sa va BYA(N)I'm well! (big smile)Comme ci, comme ça.kum SEE, kum SASo-so. (wobbly hand)Ça va mal.sa va MALNot well. (sad face)Et toi?ay TWAAnd you? (to a friend)Et vous?ay VOOAnd you? (polite, to an adult)Merci!mehr-SEEThank you!
Part 4 · Be a listening detective

Good listeners use tricks called strategies. Here are the three you'll use all year long:

WhenStrategyWhat it sounds like
Before listeningLook for clues: pictures, faces, the place.“I see a teacher and a kid at a door. I think they'll say hello!”
During listeningListen for words you already know.“I heard bonjour! I know that one!”
After listeningAsk a question if you're not sure.Peux-tu répéter, s'il te plaît?puh-TÜ ray-pay-TAY, seel tuh PLEHCan you repeat, please?
Part 5 · A song just for fun

Sometimes we listen just because it's fun, and to hear the music of French. Frère Jacques is a very old French song — more than 200 years old! You might know it in English as “Are you sleeping, Brother John?” Listen to the French words. Which sounds are new to your ears?

Did you hear “Dormez-vous?” That's the polite “you”! In the song, someone is speaking politely to Brother Jacques, a monk. Even in songs, French speakers are polite!

Surprising factOn September 25 every year, people across Ontario celebrate Franco-Ontarian Day. They raise a green and white flag with a lily flower (the lys, a symbol of French-speaking people) and a trillium (Ontario's official flower). The flag was first raised in 1975 in Sudbury — the same city where Léa lives! Green stands for summer and white for winter.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Léa said Salut to Noah but Bonjour, Madame to her teacher. What clue told Léa which greeting to use?
Stretch
If you hear someone say Salut! while they're putting on their coat and walking to the door, do they mean “hi” or “bye”? How do you know? What did you look at?
Challenge
Listen to Bonjourbo(n)-ZHOORHello and Bonsoirbo(n)-SWARGood evening. Which part sounds the same? Now listen to Bonne nuitbunn NWEEGood night. What do you think bon and bonne mean? Why might there be two ways to say it?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Use listening clues to sort French greetings into hello or goodbye, friend or adult.

Materials

  • 2 paper plates or index cards per player
  • Crayons
  • This page (for audio)
  • Optional: a stuffed animal to play “the teacher”

Steps

  1. Your child draws a waving hello hand on one card and a goodbye hand on another. On two more, draw a child (friend) and a grown-up (adult).
  2. Parent plays one phrase at a time from Part 2 and Part 3 (in a random order).
  3. After each phrase, your child holds up hello or goodbye. For Salut, they must ask “Are they arriving or leaving?” — that's the “ask a question” strategy!
  4. Round 2: parent acts out a mini-scene (arriving at the door, leaving with a coat, meeting the “teacher” teddy) and says the greeting. Child holds up friend or adult.
  5. Swap roles: your child says a greeting, and you hold up the cards. Get some wrong on purpose and let them correct you!
  6. Record each round below.

Complete in Mon cahier de français (or type/dictate below). Your child may dictate while you write.

Part A — Draw and label

Draw two pictures: (1) you greeting a friend, (2) you greeting a teacher or a neighbour. Under each, write the greeting with help: Salut! or Bonjour, Madame / Monsieur! Explain your choice in one sentence.

Part B — Feelings faces

Part C — My detective notes

Homework · À la maison

1 · The Bonjour Challenge

For 5 days, greet every family member in French every morning (Bonjour, Maman! Bonjour, Papa!) and say goodbye in French at bedtime (Bonne nuit!). Keep a tally on the fridge. How many French greetings did the family say by Friday?

2 · Family interview

Ask a grandparent, parent or neighbour: “How do you say hello in your first language? Is there a polite way and a friendly way?” Compare with French. Many languages — Spanish, German, Hindi, Yoruba, Korean — also have a polite “you”!

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Why do you think people invented polite words and friendly words? Would the world be different if everyone talked to everyone the same way?
  2. Babies understand “hello” before they can talk. How do you think a baby figures out what a greeting means?
  3. If you could invent a brand-new greeting for your family — a word plus a gesture — what would it be, and what would it mean?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 2 · Unit 2 · Mon école

Écoute bien! Les consignes de la classe

Follow the instructions! Classroom French

A1.3A2.1A2.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Imagine a teacher says a sentence you've never heard before — in a language you're still learning — and everyone in the class stands up. You don't know the words… but now you know what they meant!

Puzzle: can you understand an instruction without understanding every word? How many clues can you collect from the speaker's voice, hands, eyes and what the other people are doing?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A1.3Understand short French instructions and classroom words when I have pictures, gestures and objects to help me.
  • A2.1Use interactive listening strategies: watch the speaker, copy what others do, and show that I'm listening (eyes, nodding).
  • A2.2Respond to a request with an action, a word or a gesture (e.g., give the right object, point, stand up).

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Why this lesson matters

In a real immersion classroom, the teacher speaks French almost all day from Day 1. Children survive — and thrive — because they learn to read the situation. This lesson trains that skill and gives your child the 15 most common classroom instructions (consignes). You will use them for the rest of the year, so you are learning them too.

Preparation
  • Collect real objects: a pencil, eraser, scissors, glue, a book, crayons, a backpack, a pencil case. Put them in a box — this is your boîte mystère (mystery box).
  • Practise the instruction phrases in Part 2 with the speaker button. Choose one gesture per instruction and use it every time (e.g., hand cupped behind the ear for Écoute).
How to teach it
  1. Say it, show it, do it. For each instruction: say the French, do the gesture, then do the action yourself. Then say it again and let your child do it.
  2. After 3–4 repetitions, drop the gesture and just say the words. Can your child still do it? That's the real test.
  3. Play Jacques a dit (Simon Says) — see Classwork. It is the #1 game in Grade 1 immersion classrooms.
You can say“In French, we'll use our detective eyes. If you don't understand, look at my hands and my face. If you're still not sure, you can ask me: Peux-tu répéter? — can you repeat?”
Watch for this misconceptionYour child may freeze because they don't understand every word. Reassure them: “You don't need every word. Grab the one word you know and guess the rest.” Praise good guesses loudly, even when they're wrong: “Great detective thinking!”
Watch for this misconceptionLivre (book) and libre (free), crayon (pencil in Canada!) and English “crayon”: in Canadian French, un crayon usually means a pencil. A crayon (wax) is un crayon de cire, and a colour pencil is un crayon de couleur. Point to the real object every time.
How you'll know it clickedYou can say any of the instructions without a gesture and your child responds correctly at least 8 times out of 10. When they don't understand, they use a strategy (watch you, ask you to repeat) instead of shutting down.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · My pencil case

Léa opens her pencil case — in French, her coffre à crayons (in France they say trousse). Let's look inside! Tap each word, then find the real object in your house.

Les objets de la classe · Classroom objects

un crayonuh(n) kreh-YO(N)a pencilune gomme / une effaceün GUM / ün eh-FASSan eraserdes ciseauxday see-ZOHscissorsde la colleduh la KOLLsome glueun livreuh(n) LEEVRa bookun cahieruh(n) ka-YAYa notebookdes crayons de couleurday kreh-YO(N) duh koo-LUHRcoloured pencilsun sac à dosuh(n) sak a DOHa backpackune règleün REHGLa rulerune chaiseün SHEHZa chairune tableün TABLa tableun tableauuh(n) ta-BLOHa board (whiteboard)
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Did you hear that some words start with un and some with une? In French, every object is either a “boy word” or a “girl word” — linguists call it masculine and feminine. A chair is a girl word (une chaise) and a book is a boy word (un livre). Nobody knows exactly why! Even French adults just learn it word by word.
Part 2 · Instructions — les consignes

Teachers say these every single day. Listen, copy the gesture, and do the action!

FrenchGesture to useAction
Écoute.ay-KOOTListen.Hand cupped behind your earStop and listen

Part 3 · Listen to the whole classroom

Now listen to Madame Diallo's class. Before you listen, use your before strategy: what do you think will happen in a classroom in the morning? During listening, raise your hand every time you hear a word you know!

Did you notice that Madame Diallo says Assieds-toi to one child, but Asseyez-vous to the whole class? When a teacher talks to everybody, the words change a little, like a costume. Listen for the -ez sound at the end: that often means “all of you”.

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?The game Jacques a dit (“Jacques said”) is the French version of Simon Says. Kids in Ontario, Quebec, France and Belgium all play it the same way. Why Jacques? For hundreds of years it was one of the most common names in France — that's also why it's the name in Frère Jacques!
Part 4 · Showing I'm listening

Good listeners don't just use their ears. They use their whole body:

  • Eyes look at the speaker.
  • Body is calm and turned toward the speaker.
  • Head nods when you understand.
  • Mouth is closed while the other person talks — then you can answer!

And if you don't understand, it's smart (not silly!) to say: Je ne comprends pas.zhuh nuh ko(n)-PRA(N) paI don't understand. or Peux-tu répéter, s'il te plaît?puh-TÜ ray-pay-TAY, seel tuh PLEHCan you repeat, please?

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Your teacher says “Prends ton livre” and holds up a book. Which clue helped you more: the word livre or the book in her hand? Could you do it with only one of those clues?
Stretch
Madame Diallo says “Assieds-toi” to Léa and “Asseyez-vous” to the class. Try to find another pair in Part 3 where the words change when she talks to everyone. What sound do you hear at the end?
Challenge
You hear a brand-new instruction: Ferme la porte, s'il te plaît.fehrm la PORT, seel tuh PLEHClose the door, please. and the teacher is looking at the open door. What do you think porte means? What do you think you should do? Explain your detective clues.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Respond to French instructions with actions, first with gestures and then without.

Materials

  • The boîte mystère (a box with classroom objects)
  • A soft toy “teacher”
  • Timer (optional)

Steps

  1. Round 1 — Jacques a dit. Parent gives instructions from Part 2. If you start with Jacques a dit…zhak a DEEJacques says… your child does it. If not, they freeze! Start with gestures, then without.
  2. Round 2 — Mystery box. Parent says Donne-moi un crayon / Montre-moi les ciseaux. Child reaches in and finds the right object.
  3. Round 3 — Speed round. Time how many correct actions your child does in 1 minute. Repeat on Friday — can they beat their score?
  4. Round 4 — Swap! Your child becomes the teacher and gives you instructions in French. (This also builds their speaking!)
  5. Record the results.

Homework · À la maison

1 · French-only tidy-up

At home this week, give three everyday instructions only in French: Viens ici, Assieds-toi, Range tes affaires, and Donne-moi… at the table. Note which ones your child understood without English.

2 · Label hunt

Put sticky notes with French labels on 6 objects at home: la table, la chaise, la porte, le livre, la fenêtre (window), le lit (bed). Each time your child passes one, they say the word.

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Dogs can learn to “sit” in any language. Is a dog understanding the word, or something else? How is that different from what you do?
  2. Why do you think a pencil is a “boy word” and a chair is a “girl word” in French? Do you think it has anything to do with boys and girls at all?
  3. If you visited a country where you didn't know a single word, what would be the first three things you'd want to learn to say?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 3 · Unit 3 · Mon corps

Tête, épaules… J'écoute avec mon corps

Head, shoulders and songs: listening with my body

A1.2A1.3A2.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Here's something strange: people who don't speak any French can learn a French song in one afternoon — and remember it for 50 years. But if you gave them a list of the same words to memorise, they'd forget them by dinner.

Why do you think songs stick in our brains so much better than lists? What does music do that a list can't? Let's test it this week.

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A1.2Explain my purpose for listening to a song: for fun, and to hear and repeat French sounds.
  • A1.3Understand the names of body parts and simple actions when I hear them with gestures and pictures.
  • A2.2Respond to what I hear by touching, pointing and moving the right body part.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The idea

This week uses Total Physical Response (TPR), a well-researched method in which children learn words by moving in response to them. It's the most effective way to learn vocabulary at age 6, and it requires zero French from you — just the speaker buttons and enthusiasm.

Steps
  1. Monday: play each body word (Part 1). Touch the body part as you hear it. Your child copies. Then you say the word; your child touches.
  2. Tuesday: learn the chant in Part 2. Say it slowly with the Slow voice, then at normal speed, then fast! Children love going faster and faster.
  3. Wednesday: play Jacques a dit with body parts, and the monster game (Classwork).
  4. Throughout: whenever your child is getting dressed or in the bath, name body parts in French.
You can say“Today your body is going to learn French. Your brain will remember what your hands and feet do! Touch… la tête!”
Watch for this misconceptionFrench uses le/la/les in front of body parts (la tête, le nez, les yeux). Don't explain grammar; just always say the little word with the noun, so your child learns them as a pair. “La tête”, never just “tête”.
Watch for this misconceptionOne eye is un œil (uh-NUHY) but two eyes are les yeux (lay-ZYUH) — a completely different word! This surprises everyone. Celebrate it: “French has a secret word for two eyes!”
How you'll know it clickedYou say a body part (without touching your own) and your child touches the right one on themselves, at least 10 of 12 correctly. They can also say why they listen to songs: “To have fun and to learn French sounds.”

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Mon corps (my body)

Stand up! Listen to each word and touch that part of your body. Go slowly at first, then faster.

Les parties du corps · Body parts

la têtela TEHTthe headles cheveuxlay shuh-VUHthe hairles yeuxlay-ZYUHthe eyesle nezluh NAYthe nosela bouchela BOOSHthe mouthles oreilleslay-zo-REYthe earsles épauleslay-zay-POHLthe shouldersle ventreluh VA(N)TRthe tummyles braslay BRAthe armsles mainslay MA(N)the handsles genouxlay zhuh-NOOthe kneesles jambeslay ZHA(N)Bthe legsles piedslay PYAYthe feetles doigtslay DWAthe fingers
Part 2 · A chant to move to

This is a traditional kind of French action chant. Touch each body part as you say it. Start slow, then go faster each time!

Why are we listening to this chant? Not for information — you already know where your nose is! We listen for two reasons: because it's fun, and because it lets us hear and copy French sounds. Listen for the “eu” sound in deux and genoux… no wait, genoux has “ou”! Can you hear the difference between deux (duh) and genoux (zhuh-NOO)?

Surprising factYour body has more than 600 muscles, and you use about 100 of them just to speak! Your tongue, lips, jaw and throat all move together. When you learn French, your mouth muscles learn new moves — like the round-lipped u in tu that doesn't exist in English. You are training your mouth like an athlete!
Part 3 · Actions!

Now let's make body parts do things. Listen and act it out.

Touche ta tête.toosh ta TEHTTouch your head.Tape des mains.tap day MA(N)Clap your hands.Saute!SOHTJump!Tourne!TOORNTurn around!Lève les bras.lehv lay BRALift your arms.Ferme les yeux.fehrm lay-ZYUHClose your eyes.Ouvre la bouche.oovr la BOOSHOpen your mouth.Marche.MARSHWalk.Arrête!a-REHTStop!
Part 4 · Listening story: The Friendly Monster

Before listening: This is a story about a monster. Look at your hands — you're going to draw it as you listen! During: Draw exactly what you hear. After: Compare your drawing with the English — did you get it right?

How many number words did you hear? une, deux, trois, quatre — one, two, three, four. You'll learn to count properly next unit, but your ears already caught them!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Why is it easier to remember la tête when you touch your head while saying it? What is your hand doing to help your brain?
Stretch
In the story, Mimi has trois yeux. You know les yeux means eyes. What does trois probably mean? How did you figure it out? (Hint: count Mimi's eyes in your drawing.)
Challenge
One eye = un œil. Two eyes = les yeux. In English, one mouse = mouse, two = mice. Can you think of other English words that change completely when there's more than one? Why might languages do this?

  2. Compare the drawing with the English line by line. Tick each correct part.

  4. Play Jacques a dit with the action phrases from Part 3 for 5 minutes.

Draw yourself (big!). Parent plays 8 body-part words, one at a time. Child draws an arrow and copies the French word: la tête, le nez, la bouche, les yeux, les bras, les mains, les jambes, les pieds.

Homework · À la maison

1 · Bath time and dressing French

Every day this week, during bath time or getting dressed, the parent names 5 body parts in French and your child points, or the reverse. Try one day completely without English!

2 · Song for the family

Teach Tête, épaules, genoux, pieds to one family member who doesn't know it. Your child is the teacher! Record a short video if you like — it's great for the portfolio.

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Why do people all over the world sing songs to babies, even before babies understand words?
  2. Mimi has three eyes. Would three eyes help or confuse your brain? Why do most animals have two?
  3. If your body could only learn one more language through movement — dance, sign language or French actions — which would you choose, and why?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 4 · Unit 4 · Ma famille, ma maison

L'histoire de ma famille

Family stories: listening before, during and after

A1.1A1.3A3.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Every family has traditions — special foods, special days, special words that only your family uses. In Franco-Ontarian families, some children stay up past midnight on Christmas Eve to eat a giant family feast called the réveillon.

Puzzle: réveillon comes from the French word réveiller, which means “to wake up”. Why would a midnight dinner be named after waking up? Make a guess before you listen!

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A1.1Use my before-during-after strategies on a longer story: predict from the title and pictures, listen for family words, retell after.
  • A1.3Understand a simple spoken story about a family, with familiar words and pictures.
  • A3.1Learn about family traditions in French-speaking communities in Ontario and compare them with my own family.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

What's new this week

The story in The Lesson is longer than anything your child has heard so far. That's deliberate: it trains listening stamina and the before/during/after strategies. Your child won't understand every word — the goal is the gist (main idea).

How to run the listening
  1. Before: read the title and look at the family words. Ask: “What do you think the story will be about? Who will be in it?” Write predictions down.
  2. During (first listen): play the whole story once with Play all. Child just listens, eyes closed, and raises a finger for each family word they hear.
  3. During (second listen): play line by line. After each line, ask one question in English: “Who is this about?”
  4. After: child retells the story in English with the family puppet or drawings. Then check predictions.
You can say“We don't need to understand every word. Let's catch the big fish — the important words — and let the little fish swim away.”
Cultural noteFamily words change with a boy/girl ending: le frère (brother) / la sœur (sister), le grand-père / la grand-mère. Canadian children often say papi/mamie or pépère/mémère for grandpa/grandma. All are correct!
Watch for this misconceptionParents in French means parents, but les grands-parents means grandparents, not “big parents”. Children sometimes translate word by word: it's a good chance to talk about how word pieces combine (grand = big/grand).
How you'll know it clickedAfter the second listen, your child can retell the story in English with at least 4 correct details (who, what they did, when) and name 5 family members in French when you point to pictures.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Ma famille (my family)

Let's meet the family words. Use a family photo, or draw your own family, and point to each person as you hear the word.

La famille · Family

la famillela fa-MEE-yuhthe familyla maman / la mèrela ma-MA(N) / la MEHRthe mom / the motherle papa / le pèreluh pa-PA / luh PEHRthe dad / the fatherle frèreluh FREHRthe brotherla sœurla SUHRthe sisterle bébéluh bay-BAYthe babyla grand-mère / mamiela gra(n)-MEHR / ma-MEEthe grandmother / grandmale grand-père / papiluh gra(n)-PEHR / pa-PEEthe grandfather / grandpala tantela TA(N)Tthe auntl'oncleLO(N)KLthe unclele cousin / la cousineluh koo-ZA(N) / la koo-ZEENthe cousin (boy / girl)le chien / le chatluh SHYA(N) / luh SHAthe dog / the cat
Part 2 · Listening story: Le réveillon de Léa

Before you listen: Look at the title. Léa — you know her! Réveillon — the midnight feast. What do you predict will happen? Who might come?

After listening: Who was at mamie's house? What did papi do? What happened at midnight? Were your predictions right?

Answer to the Wonder HookThe answer to our puzzle: long ago, families went to church at midnight on Christmas Eve, then came home very late and had a feast. Everyone had to stay awake (rester éveillé) — so the feast was named réveillon! Traditional foods in Franco-Ontarian and Québécois families include tourtière (a spiced meat pie), ragoût de boulettes (meatball stew) and bûche de Noël (a cake shaped like a log).
Part 3 · Families are different — and that's great!

French-speaking families in Ontario come from many places. Some have lived here for more than 400 years. Others arrived recently from Haiti, Senegal, Lebanon, Morocco, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Belgium or France. Each family brings its own traditions:

FamilyA tradition
A Franco-Ontarian family in HearstA New Year's Day blessing: children ask their father or grandfather for his blessing — la bénédiction paternelle.
A Haitian family in TorontoOn January 1st they eat soup joumou, a pumpkin soup that celebrates Haiti's independence in 1804.
A Lebanese family in OttawaBig family meals with dozens of small dishes shared by everyone.
Your familyWhat's your special tradition?
Surprising factSoup joumou was added to UNESCO's list of the world's important cultural heritage in 2021. Haiti is one of the largest French-speaking countries in the Americas, and Haitian Creole and French are both its official languages.
Part 4 · Where are you? Listening for “chez”

Did you notice the little word chez in the story? Chez mamie means “at grandma's house”. French doesn't need the word “house” — chez does the job! chez moishay MWAat my house chez papishay pa-PEEat grandpa's chez Noahshay no-Aat Noah's

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Which family words helped you understand the story the most? If you only heard those words and nothing else, could you still tell what the story was about?
Stretch
Before you listened, you made a prediction. Was it right? What clue made you guess it? Would the story have been harder without the title?
Challenge
Grand-mère = grand + mère. Grand-père = grand + père. What would a grand frère be? And a petit frère? (Hint: petit = small.) Explain how you figured it out.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Listen to descriptions of a family and build the family tree from what you hear.

Materials

  • Paper cut into 10 small cards
  • Crayons
  • Tape or glue
  • Large sheet of paper

Steps

  1. Child draws 10 family members on small cards (mom, dad, brother, sister, baby, grandma, grandpa, aunt, uncle, cousin).
  2. Parent plays each word from Part 1 in random order. Child finds the card and holds it up.
  3. Parent reads the story line 3 and 4 again. Child places those cards on the big sheet — this is Léa's family tree!
  4. Now do your family: parent says (with the speaker buttons as needed) Voici ta grand-mère… Voici ton oncle… Child places cards to build their own family tree.
  5. Record which words were easy and which were tricky.

Assignment · Le devoir

Notebook assignment — drawings plus dictated or copied French.

Part A — Story map

Divide a page into 4 boxes: Who? Where? What happened? How did Léa feel? Draw the answer in each box. Parent adds the French word from the story (la famille, Ottawa, le réveillon, contente).

Part B — Strategy check

Complete: “Before I listened, I… During listening, I… After listening, I…” (child dictates).

Part C — Compare traditions

Draw one tradition from Léa's family and one from your own family. Write (or dictate) how they are the same and how they are different.

Homework · À la maison

1 · Interview a grandparent or elder

Ask: “What special family tradition did you have when you were six?” Your child tells you the answer in English, then you both find 2 French words from this lesson that fit the story.

2 · Family photo tour

Show family photos. Child says one French word for each person: ma sœur, mon oncle, ma grand-mère. (mon = my for boy-words; ma = my for girl-words.)

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Why do you think families keep doing the same tradition every year, even for hundreds of years?
  2. If your family moved to another country, which tradition would you never want to lose? Why that one?
  3. Some words, like chez, don't exist in English. What might happen to a word that no language wants to use anymore?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 5 · Unit 5 · L'hiver

La météo à la télé: je suis détective des médias

Media detectives: the winter weather report

A1.3A1.4A3.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Every morning, millions of Canadians listen to someone they've never met tell them whether to wear boots. That person has never seen your house and doesn't know your name — but you still trust them!

Puzzle: how does a weather reporter on TV or radio make you believe them? Is it their voice, their pictures, their clothes, their music? And could they ever get it wrong?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A1.3Understand a short French weather report and winter words with pictures and symbols.
  • A1.4Say what I think and feel about a short media message (a weather report, an ad) and how it was made — using words, faces or thumbs.
  • A3.1Learn about the Carnaval de Québec and winter traditions in French-speaking communities, and connect them to my own winters.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

What's “media” for a 6-year-old?

A media text is any message made to reach many people: a TV show, a radio ad, a video, a poster, a cereal box. The Ontario curriculum asks Grade 1 children to start noticing how these messages are made (music, pictures, voice) and to share an opinion. This week we use a weather report because it's short, repetitive and full of visual clues.

Steps
  1. Watch a real French weather report together if you can (Radio-Canada's local news or TFO often has one — search “météo” with your city). Even 30 seconds counts. Turn the sound on, then off: what can you still understand?
  2. Learn the weather and winter words in Parts 1–2 with gestures.
  3. Listen to Météo-Mimi (Part 3) — our pretend weather report.
  4. Talk about the media questions in Part 4 using thumbs up / sideways / down.
You can say“A weather report is made by people who want us to watch and believe them. Let's be media detectives and figure out their tricks!”
Canadian FrenchIn Canada, many French speakers say Il fait soleil for “it's sunny”; in France people usually say Il fait beau or Il y a du soleil. All are correct. Canadians also say la tuque (winter hat) and les mitaines (mittens) — in France these are le bonnet and les moufles.
How you'll know it clickedYour child can listen to a weather report and tell you, using a symbol card, what the weather will be and what to wear. They can also give one opinion about the report and one reason (“I liked it because the music was happy”).

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Quel temps fait-il? (What's the weather?)

La météo · The weather

Il fait froid.eel feh FRWAIt's cold. (hug yourself and shiver)Il fait chaud.eel feh SHOHIt's hot. (fan your face)Il fait soleil.eel feh so-LEYIt's sunny. (arms in a big circle)Il neige.eel NEHZHIt's snowing. (fingers wiggling down)Il pleut.eel PLUHIt's raining. Part 2 · Les vêtements d'hiver (winter clothes)

L'hiver · Winter

Surprising factThe coldest temperature ever measured in Canada was −63 °C in Snag, Yukon, in 1947. It was so cold that people said their breath made a hissing sound as it froze, and voices carried much farther than usual through the icy air.
Part 3 · Météo-Mimi (a pretend weather report)

Before: Look at the symbols you learned. What do you think the weather will be in January? During: Hold up the right symbol card for each city. After: What should you wear?

Part 4 · Media detective questions

Think about a weather report on TV (a real one, or Mimi's). Show your answer with your thumb 👍 / sideways / 👎, then explain.

  • Did you like the report? Why? (The voice? The pictures? The music?)
  • What did the reporter do to help you understand? (Maps, symbols, pointing, smiling?)
  • Why do weather reporters smile so much, even when the news is bad weather?
  • Who is the report made for? Kids? Grown-ups? Everyone?

Useful French for opinions: J'aime ça!zhehm SAI like it! Je n'aime pas ça.zhuh nehm pa SAI don't like it. C'est drôle!seh DROHLIt's funny! C'est super!seh sü-PEHRIt's great! C'est ennuyant.seh-ta(n)-nwee-YA(N)It's boring.

Part 5 · Le Carnaval de Québec

Every winter, Quebec City holds one of the biggest winter festivals in the world: the Carnaval de Québec. Its mascot is a giant snowman with a red tuque and a colourful woven sash called a ceinture fléchée. His name is Bonhomme Carnavalbo-NUM kar-na-VALBonhomme (the snowman mascot). People go sliding on ice slides, watch snow sculptures, ride in canoes across the icy St. Lawrence River, and eat tire sur la neige — hot maple syrup poured on snow that turns into chewy taffy!

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?The Carnaval de Québec in its modern form started in 1955. Bonhomme Carnaval lives in an ice palace built fresh every year from blocks of ice. And the canoe race across the frozen St. Lawrence River comes from a real old job: long ago, people delivered mail and supplies across the river in winter by pushing canoes over the ice!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Mimi said Il neige for Sudbury. What should Léa wear in Sudbury today? Name three things in French.
Stretch
If you turned the sound off on a weather report, could you still understand it? What would you use? If you turned the picture off (like radio), what would help you?
Challenge
Weather reporters are sometimes wrong. Why do you think that happens? Should they tell us when they're not sure? How could they say it?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Listen to weather reports and dress a paper doll, then make and present your own weather report.

Materials

  • Paper doll (draw one) and paper clothes: tuque, mitaines, foulard, bottes, manteau, t-shirt, shorts, sunglasses
  • Weather symbol cards (draw 6: sun, snow, rain, wind, cloud, thermometer)
  • A “microphone” (a spoon or marker)

Steps

  1. Make the weather symbol cards and paper clothes together. Label each in French.
  2. Parent plays one line of Météo-Mimi at a time; child holds up the right weather card and dresses the paper doll for that city.
  3. Parent invents new reports: À Toronto, il fait chaud! Child dresses the doll (shorts!).
  4. Child becomes the weather reporter with the microphone and gives a one-line report: Aujourd'hui, il ___.
  5. Media talk: rate Mimi's report and your own with thumbs, and give one reason each.

CityWeather I heardClothes I chose

Assignment · Le devoir

Notebook work over the week.

Part A — Weather diary

For 5 days, draw today's weather and write the sentence with help: Aujourd'hui, il fait ___ / il neige / il pleut. Use the speaker to check.

Part B — My opinion

Watch a short French or English kids' ad or weather report. Draw your favourite part. Complete: J'aime ça / Je n'aime pas ça parce que… (because…) — reason in English is fine.

Part C — Carnaval poster

Draw Bonhomme Carnaval and one Carnaval activity. Tell how it is the same or different from what you do in winter.

Homework · À la maison

1 · Morning weather reporter

Each morning this week, your child looks out the window and gives the family a French weather report before breakfast: Bonjour! Aujourd'hui, il fait froid. Mettez vos tuques! (Put on your hats!)

2 · Real-media hunt

With a parent, find one French media message anywhere — a bilingual cereal box, a bus sign, a radio station. What is it trying to make you do or think?

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Why do you think there are no snowflakes exactly alike? Who has checked them all?
  2. If animals could make weather reports for other animals, what would a bear's report say? A bird's?
  3. Why do people in very cold places throw big winter parties instead of just staying inside?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 6 · Unit 6 · Miam!

À la cabane à sucre: j'écoute et je réponds

At the sugar shack: listening to take part

A2.1A2.2A3.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

At a cabane à sucre (sugar shack), a server walks up to your table and says “Qu'est-ce que vous voulez?” Your mom answers. Then the server turns to you and says “Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu veux?”

Puzzle: the server asked the same question twice, but with different words. Why would someone change their words depending on who they're talking to? Do you do that too, in English — maybe without noticing?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A2.1Use interactive listening strategies in a conversation: look at the speaker, listen for the question word, and ask for repetition politely.
  • A2.2Respond with understanding when someone offers me food or asks what I want (words, pointing, oui/non).
  • A3.2Notice when French speakers use tu (friends, family, children) and vous (adults we don't know, or many people), and s'il te plaît / s'il vous plaît.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Background for you

Canada produces most of the world's maple syrup, and every spring (March–April) French-speaking families visit a cabane à sucre to eat a big traditional meal and tire sur la neige (maple taffy on snow). This lesson turns that into a listening-and-responding role-play and introduces the single most important politeness rule in French: tu vs vous.

The tu / vous rule, simply
Say tu to…Say vous to…
Friends, brothers and sisters, cousins, parents, grandparents (in most families)Adults you don't know well: servers, shopkeepers, doctors, a friend's parent
Children your ageYour teacher (in most schools)
Pets and stuffed animals!Any group of two or more people — even friends
How to teach it
  1. Set up a pretend sugar shack at your table (Classwork). You are the server; use vous with the stuffed animals as “adults” and tu with your child.
  2. Emphasise listening for the question word: Qu'est-ce que (what), Combien (how many), Tu veux / Vous voulez (you want).
  3. Always wait for your child to respond before helping. Count to 5 silently. Silence is thinking time.
You can say“When someone asks you a question in French, your job is to catch the question word first. Then look at what they're pointing at or holding. Then answer — with a word, oui or non, or even just by pointing.”
Watch for this misconceptionChildren often assume vous is “rude” or “angry”. It's the opposite: it's respectful. Compare it to calling an adult “Mr. Smith” instead of “Bob”.
How you'll know it clickedIn the role-play, your child answers at least 5 food questions appropriately (with a word, oui/non or a gesture) and can tell you whether the server was using tu or vous and why.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Qu'est-ce qu'on mange? (What do we eat?)

À la cabane à sucre · At the sugar shack

These are the questions you'll hear. Listen for the question word (in bold) — it tells you what kind of answer to give.

Part 3 · Listening role-play

Before: Who will talk? (A server, a mom, a child.) What will they talk about? During: Listen for tu and vous — clap once for tu, twice for vous! After: Who got vous? Why?

Did you catch it? The server said vous to Maman (an adult he doesn't know) and tu to Samuel (a child). And Samuel said s'il vous plaît to the server — because the server is an adult he doesn't know. Samuel is very polite!

Please — to a friend or family memberPlease — to an adult you don't know, or a group
s'il te plaîtseel tuh PLEHplease (friendly)s'il vous plaîtseel voo PLEHplease (polite)
Surprising factAbout 7 out of every 10 bottles of maple syrup in the whole world come from Quebec. It takes about 40 litres of sap from maple trees to make just 1 litre of syrup! Indigenous peoples of the eastern woodlands were making maple sugar long before Europeans arrived, and taught early French settlers how to do it.
Part 4 · When you don't understand

Even adults don't always understand. In a conversation you can say:

Pardon?par-DO(N)Sorry? / Pardon?Peux-tu répéter, s'il te plaît?puh-TÜ ray-pay-TAY, seel tuh PLEHCan you repeat, please? (to a friend)Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît?poo-vay VOO ray-pay-TAY, seel voo PLEHCould you repeat, please? (polite)Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.plü la(n)t-MA(N), seel voo PLEHMore slowly, please.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
The server asked Samuel Combien de crêpes? What kind of answer did he need — a colour, a number or a yes/no? Which word told you?
Stretch
Would you say tu or vous to: your grandma? A new doctor? Your cat? Three friends at once? Explain each choice.
Challenge
Samuel is a child, but he said s'il vous plaît to the server. The server is an adult, but he said tu to Samuel. Is that fair? Why do you think grown-ups and children use different words with each other?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Take part in a sugar-shack role-play by listening to questions and responding appropriately.

Materials

  • Paper plates, cups, cutlery
  • Paper “food” (draw crêpes, ham, eggs, syrup bottle) or real snacks
  • Stuffed animals as other “customers”
  • Optional: a real maple-taffy treat (pour hot syrup on clean snow or crushed ice and roll on a popsicle stick — adult job!)

Steps

  1. Set the table. Parent is le serveur / la serveuse (server) with a notepad.
  2. Parent greets the stuffed animals using vous and your child using tu. Child claps once for tu, twice for vous.
  3. Parent asks your child each question from Part 2. Child responds (word, oui/non, number, or pointing). If stuck, child uses a Part 4 phrase.
  4. Switch: child is the server and must choose tu or vous for each customer.
  5. Record the orders below — the server writes down what each customer wanted.

Record your observations

Customertu or vous?What they orderedHow many?

Assignment · Le devoir

Notebook work with drawings and copying.

Part A — My sugar-shack plate

Draw your plate at the cabane à sucre. Label 4 foods in French (copy from Part 1). Circle your favourite.

Part B — Tu or vous? sorting

Draw or cut out pictures of 6 people (baby, teacher, grandpa, a store clerk, your friend, a police officer). Glue them into two columns: TU and VOUS. Explain one tricky choice.

Part C — What did I hear?

Parent plays the dialogue again. Child answers in English: What did Maman order? How many crêpes did Samuel want? What did he drink?

Homework · À la maison

1 · French at the table

At three family meals this week, ask your child in French: Qu'est-ce que tu veux? Tu veux de l'eau ou du lait? They must answer in French to get it (gently!).

2 · Polite hunt

Next time you're at a store or restaurant, listen together: how does the cashier talk to adults and to children? In English too — do they change their voice or words?

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Trees can't talk — but in spring, how does a maple tree “know” it's time to send sweet sap up its trunk?
  2. English used to have a “tu” too: thou! Why do you think English stopped using it?
  3. Is it possible to be polite without using any words at all? How?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 7 · Unit 7 · Les animaux

Les histoires d'animaux: je prédis en écoutant

Animal tales: predicting while I listen

A1.1A1.2A1.3
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

In English, a rooster says “cock-a-doodle-doo”. In French, it says “cocorico!” A dog says “ouaf ouaf!” and a duck says “coin-coin!”

Puzzle: French roosters and Canadian roosters are the same kind of bird. They make the same sound. So why do French speakers and English speakers hear something different? What does that tell you about ears and brains?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A1.1Predict what will happen next in a story I'm listening to, using the title, pictures and what I've heard so far — then check my prediction.
  • A1.2Name different purposes for listening: to enjoy a story, to learn facts about animals, to play a sound game.
  • A1.3Understand a spoken animal story and short animal facts with familiar words and pictures.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The skill: prediction

Good listeners are always guessing what comes next — this keeps the brain active and makes understanding much easier. This week you will stop the story at key moments and ask “What do you think will happen?” The story uses a repeated pattern so your child can predict both events and words.

Steps
  1. Learn the animal names with sounds (Part 1). Have fun — do the animal noises!
  2. Play the story (Part 3) line by line, stopping at the STOP markers to ask for predictions. Write predictions on sticky notes.
  3. Listen to the fact file (Part 4) — this is listening for information, a different purpose from the story. Discuss the difference.
You can say“Let's stop here. What do you think the beaver will say? Why do you think so? You can answer in English — the thinking is what matters.”
Watch for this misconceptionYour child may say “I don't know” to prediction questions. Model it yourself: “I think the moose will come next because the story keeps adding bigger animals.” Then ask again.
How you'll know it clickedYour child makes at least 3 predictions during the story that are based on evidence (“because it keeps happening”) and can tell you the difference between listening to a story (for fun) and listening to facts (to learn).

The Lesson · La leçon

Answer to the Wonder HookThese sound words are called onomatopoeia (onomatopées in French). Every language hears animals differently: a Japanese rooster says kokekokko and a German dog says wau wau. Our brains “hear” sounds using the sounds our own language already has!
Part 2 · Canadian animals

Les animaux du Canada · Canadian animals

le castorluh kas-TORthe beaverl'orignallo-ree-NYALthe moosel'oursLOORSthe bearle renardluh ruh-NARthe foxle loupluh LOOthe wolfle hibouluh ee-BOOthe owlle lapinluh la-PA(N)the rabbitl'écureuillay-kü-RUHYthe squirrelle raton laveurluh ra-TO(N) la-VUHRthe raccoonla mouffettela moo-FETTthe skunk
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Raton laveur means “little rat that washes” — because raccoons dip their food in water and rub it with their paws, as if washing it! And orignal (moose) comes from a Basque word — it's one of the few French words that came from Basque fishermen who sailed to Canada 500 years ago.
Part 3 · Listening story: La petite cabane dans la forêt

Before: The title means “The little cabin in the forest”. What animals live in a Canadian forest? Who do you think will be in the story? During: Stop at each STOP and predict! After: Were you right?

This story has a pattern: the same words come back again and again (Toc, toc, toc! Je peux entrer? Oui, entre!). Patterns help you predict. After two animals, you knew exactly what the next one would say!

Part 4 · Listening for facts: Le castor

Now we're listening for a different reason: to learn real facts. Listen carefully — then tell the facts back.

Surprising factBeavers' teeth really are orange! They contain iron, which makes them extra strong — strong enough to cut down a tree. And they never stop growing, so beavers must keep chewing wood to keep them short.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Which words in the story came back again and again? How did they help you guess what would happen?
Stretch
Why did the tiny owl make the cabin fall down, and not the big bear? Is that a real-life thing or a joke in the story? Why do storytellers like surprises?
Challenge
The story and the beaver fact file are both about animals. How is listening to them different? What were you doing with your brain in each one?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Act out the story with puppets, then play an animal-sound listening game.

Materials

  • Paper-bag or sock puppets (or stuffed animals): rabbit, squirrel, fox, bear, owl
  • A box or blanket for the cabin
  • Blindfold (optional)

Steps

  1. Make simple puppets or gather stuffed animals. Label each with its French name.
  2. Parent plays the story line by line; child moves the animals into the cabin. At each STOP, child predicts before you continue.
  3. Act it again: this time your child says the repeated lines (Toc, toc, toc! Je peux entrer?) and you answer Oui, entre!
  4. Qui suis-je? (Who am I?) sound game: parent plays or makes a French animal sound; child names the animal in French. Then swap.
  5. Record the predictions and whether they came true.

Notebook assignment.

Part A — Story sequence

Draw the story in 4 boxes: 1) the rabbit finds the cabin, 2) more animals come, 3) the owl arrives, 4) the cabin falls. Label each animal in French.

Part B — Beaver fact card

Draw a beaver. Write or dictate 3 facts you heard (Il a de grandes dents orange…). Parent helps copy one fact in French.

Part C — Change the story

What if a different animal arrived at the end instead of the owl — maybe a mouffette (skunk)? Tell your new ending. What would happen?

1 · Animal sounds survey

Ask 3 people who speak other languages (or look it up together) what a dog, cat and rooster say in their language. Add French and English. Which languages are most alike?

2 · Bedtime story prediction

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Do animals of the same kind “speak” with different accents in different countries? (Scientists have studied this with birds and whales — what do you think they found?)
  2. Why do so many children's stories use a pattern that repeats?
  3. If a beaver could tell the story of how it built its dam, what would it say?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 8 · Unit 8 · Le calendrier et la météo

Mes super-pouvoirs d'écoute: le calendrier

My listening superpowers: days, months and me as a listener

A1.3A1.4A2.3
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

You have now been listening to French for almost eight months. Your brain has changed in ways you can't see: it has built new paths just for French sounds.

Puzzle: how can you measure something you can't see? How could you prove to someone — or to yourself — that you're a better French listener now than in September?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A1.3Understand the days of the week, months of the year and birthdays in spoken French.
  • A1.4Give my opinion about a short media message (a birthday video message or radio ad) and how it was made.
  • A2.3(a) Describe the listening strategies that help me most; (b) say what I'm good at as a listener and what I want to improve, and make a plan.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

This week is about metacognition

Metacognition means “thinking about your own thinking”. Research consistently shows that children who reflect on how they learn become stronger learners. This week your child learns the calendar words (which you've been using in the morning routine) and then does a reflection and goal-setting session about themselves as a listener.

Steps
  1. Days and months with songs and the birthday game.
  2. Listening “then and now”: replay the Unit 1 dialogue from Lesson A1. Ask: “How much do you understand now compared to September?”
  3. Complete the Listener Self-Portrait in the Assignment — honestly, without judgement.
You can say“Everyone has listening strengths and things they're still working on — me too! Let's be scientists about ourselves. What helps you understand French the most?”
Portfolio momentIf you recorded a video in September (see Start Here → Resources), watch it now! If not, record one this week to compare in June.
Watch for this misconceptionChildren may say “I'm bad at French” when they mean “I don't understand everything.” Reframe: “Nobody understands everything — not even adults learning French. Let's look at what you can do now that you couldn't do in September.”
How you'll know it clickedYour child can name the days in order, recognise most months when heard, and tell you one listening strategy they use and one listening goal (e.g., “I want to understand faster talking”).

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Les jours de la semaine (the days of the week)

You already say these every morning! Clap once for each day as you hear it.

Les jours · Days

lundiluh(n)-DEEMondaymardimar-DEETuesdaymercredimehr-kruh-DEEWednesdayjeudizhuh-DEEThursdayvendrediva(n)-druh-DEEFridaysamedisam-DEESaturdaydimanchedee-MA(N)SHSunday

Listen to this chant. Can you hear what's special about the ending of most days? (Hint: -di!)

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?-di comes from an old Latin word, dies, meaning “day”. So lundi is “Moon-day” (Lune), mardi is “Mars-day”, mercredi is “Mercury-day”, jeudi is “Jupiter-day” and vendredi is “Venus-day”. English does it too: Monday is “Moon-day”!
Part 2 · Les mois de l'année (the months)

Les mois · Months

janvierzha(n)-VYAYJanuaryfévrierfay-vree-YAYFebruarymarsMARSSMarchavrila-VREELAprilmaiMEHMayjuinZHWA(N)Junejuilletzhwee-YEHJulyaoûtOOTAugustseptembresep-TA(N)BRSeptemberoctobreok-TOBROctobernovembreno-VA(N)BRNovemberdécembreday-SA(N)BRDecember

Notice: in French, days and months do not start with a capital letter — unless they start a sentence. Surprise!

Part 3 · Les anniversaires (birthdays)
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?In Canada, French speakers usually say Bonne fête! for “Happy birthday!”, and many families sing Gens du pays, a famous Québécois song by Gilles Vigneault, instead of the “Happy Birthday” tune. In France, people say Joyeux anniversaire! Same language, different habits!
Part 4 · A media message: a radio ad

Listen to this pretend radio ad. Media detective: What does it want you to do? How does it try to make you excited?

Talk about it: Which day and month is the festival? Why does the ad say Les amis! twice? Why does it say gratuit (free)? Would you go? What would make the ad even better?

Part 5 · How I listen — my super-powers

Think back to September. Which of these can you do now? Stand up for each one!

  • I can follow the morning routine without English.
  • I can do what someone asks me in French (Assieds-toi, Donne-moi…).
  • I can understand a whole short story if I have pictures.
  • I can guess the meaning of new words from clues.
  • I ask Peux-tu répéter? when I need it.

Warm-up
Which listening strategy do you use the most? Is it looking at pictures, listening for words you know, predicting, or asking for help?
Stretch
What makes French harder to understand: when people talk fast, when there are no pictures, when there are new words, or something else? Why?
Challenge
A radio ad has no pictures. What does the ad do with its voice and words to make you picture the festival in your head? Could you make a radio ad for your birthday party?

Écouter · Listening — Lesson 9 · Unit 9 · Ma communauté, notre francophonie

Ma communauté francophone: des voix d'ici et d'ailleurs

Our Franco-Ontarian community: voices from near and far

A3.1A3.2A1.4A2.3
1–2 weeks · 5–8 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

There's a city in Africa where more people speak French every day than in Paris. There's an island in the Caribbean where children learn French and Creole at school. And there are towns in northern Ontario where almost everyone speaks French at the grocery store.

Puzzle: French started in France. How do you think it travelled across oceans to Africa, the Caribbean and Ontario — and why didn't it change into exactly the same French everywhere?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • A3.1Using what I hear, learn about French-speaking communities in Ontario (their places, celebrations and people) and connect them to my own life and community.
  • A3.2Recognise how French speakers greet and thank people in the community, and when they use tu or vous, Madame or Monsieur.
  • A1.4Share my opinion about a short community media message (a festival announcement) and how it was made.
  • A2.3Look back on my whole year of listening: my best strategies, my strengths, and my goal for Grade 2.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Culminating lesson

This is the year's final listening lesson and can easily stretch over two weeks around June 24 (Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day, a major francophone celebration). Your child hears “voices” of French speakers from Ontario and around the world, meets community helpers, and does a year-end listening reflection.

Try to do this in real life
  • Attend a local Franco-Ontarian event (June 24 celebrations happen in Ottawa, Sudbury, Toronto, Windsor, Hamilton, Timmins, Hearst, Welland and many other places).
  • Visit a French-language library section, a francophone bakery or a French church or community centre. Let your child hear French spoken by real people and practise Bonjour, Madame / Monsieur and Merci.
You can say“French isn't just a school subject. It's a language that real families, kids, grandparents, singers and bakers use every day — right here in Ontario. Let's go meet some of them!”
Watch for this misconceptionYour child may hear French that sounds different from the speaker buttons (accents from Ottawa, Quebec, Haiti, France or Senegal). That's wonderful! Explain: “Just like English sounds different in Australia, Texas and Scotland, French has many accents. All of them are real French.”
How you'll know it clickedYour child can name at least 2 places in Ontario where people speak French, one francophone celebration, and 2 countries outside Canada where French is spoken. They greet a French-speaking adult politely (Bonjour, Madame) in real life or role-play.

Part 1 · Voices from Ontario

Listen to four children introduce themselves. Before: What do you think they'll tell us? (name, age, city…) During: Point to each city on the map of Ontario (use a real map or a map app). After: Who lives closest to you?

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Chloé said Allô! Many French Canadians say Allô as a friendly “hi”, not only on the phone. You'll hear it all over Ontario and Quebec.

Surprising factThere are about 320 million French speakers in the world, and more than half of them live in Africa. French speakers call the whole French-speaking world la francophonie. It celebrates its own international day on March 20.
Part 3 · Community helpers — tu or vous?

Listen to Léa talking to people in her community. Clap once for tu, twice for vous.

Léa used vous and Madame / Monsieur with the adults. The adults used tu with Léa. That's the rule you learned at the sugar shack — and it works everywhere in the francophonie!
