Lessons · Leçons

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 1 · Unit 1 · Bonjour!

Je me présente!

All about me: introducing myself

B1.2B2.1B3.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

When you meet someone new, what's the very first thing you want them to know about you? Your name? Your age? That you love dinosaurs?

Puzzle: In just three short French sentences, could you tell a stranger enough about yourself that they'd want to be your friend? Which three facts would you choose — and why those?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B1.2Say a planned and practised introduction about myself: my name, my age, how I feel, and one thing I like.
  • B2.1Take turns in a conversation: wait, look at the speaker, and speak loudly enough to be heard.
  • B3.2Use greetings and goodbyes correctly (Salut / Bonjour, Madame / Au revoir), with a handshake, wave or smile as appropriate.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The big idea

Your child will learn their first “speech”: a four-sentence self-introduction. It will be used and expanded all year (with family in Unit 4, likes in Unit 6, etc.). The sentences are formulas — chunks to memorise as whole phrases, not grammar to analyse.

Teaching sequence
  1. Model it yourself first. Introduce yourself in French using the speaker button to check each line. Your child sees that you are brave too.
  2. Echo, then chorus, then solo. Your child repeats after you (echo), then you say it together (chorus), then your child says it alone (solo).
  3. Use a talking object. Only the person holding the “talking stick” (a spoon, a toy microphone) may speak. This teaches turn-taking (B2.1) naturally.
  4. End each session with a handshake: Au revoir, Madame / Monsieur!
You can say“In French, when you meet someone, you say Bonjour, shake hands or wave, and tell them your name. Let me show you. Bonjour! Je m'appelle Maman. J'ai… beaucoup d'années!” (Humour helps!)
Watch for this misconceptionJe m'appelle literally means “I call myself”. Children sometimes say “Je m'appelle est Léa” (mixing English “my name is”). Recast gently: “Je m'appelle Léa. Just the name after it!”
Watch for this misconceptionJ'ai six ans means literally “I have six years”. Children often say Je suis six (English thinking). Recast: “Ah, tu as six ans! J'ai six ans.” Explain once, playfully: “In French, you have your years, like having candies!”
How you'll know it clickedYour child can stand up, greet you, and say all four sentences of their introduction without help, loudly and clearly, then say goodbye appropriately. They wait for their turn in a conversation.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · My four magic sentences

Here's how Léa introduces herself. Listen to each sentence, then say it yourself — with your information!

Part 2 · Numbers for my age
J'ai cinq ans.zhay sa(n)k A(N)I am five.J'ai six ans.zhay see ZA(N)I am six.J'ai sept ans.zhay seh TA(N)I am seven.J'ai huit ans.zhay wee TA(N)I am eight.

Listen: when you say six ans, the x makes a z sound — “see-ZAN”. That's called a liaison: two words holding hands!

Part 3 · How do I feel?
A boy says…A girl says…Meaning
Je suis content.zhuh swee ko(n)-TA(N)I'm happy.Je suis contente.zhuh swee ko(n)-TA(N)TI'm happy.happy
Je suis triste.zhuh swee TREESTI'm sad.Je suis triste.zhuh swee TREESTI'm sad.sad (same for both!)
Je suis fatigué.zhuh swee fa-tee-GAYI'm tired.Je suis fatiguée.zhuh swee fa-tee-GAYI'm tired.tired (sounds the same!)
Je suis fâché.zhuh swee fa-SHAYI'm angry.Je suis fâchée.zhuh swee fa-SHAYI'm angry.angry
Je suis nerveux.zhuh swee nehr-VUHI'm nervous.Je suis nerveuse.zhuh swee nehr-VUHZI'm nervous.nervous
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?In French, some describing words change their spelling (and sometimes their sound) depending on whether a boy or a girl is talking. Content and contente sound different — can you hear the “t” at the end of contente? But fatigué and fatiguée sound exactly the same; only the spelling changes!
Part 4 · A real conversation

Now let's put it together with a partner. Practise with your parent, a puppet or a teddy. Remember: wait for your turn!

Part 5 · Greetings with your body

In French-speaking places, greetings come with actions:

  • Handshake (une poignée de main) — common with adults, especially the first time you meet.
  • Wave (un salut de la main) — with friends, and from far away.
  • La bise — in Quebec and France, family and close friends greet each other with a light kiss on both cheeks! (In France, in some regions, it's 3 or even 4 kisses!)
Cultural factIn Canada, la bise is usually two kisses — one on each cheek — starting with the right cheek. You never have to do it if you don't want to; a smile and Bonjour are always perfect.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Which of your four sentences was the easiest to say? Which was the trickiest? Why?
Stretch
Noah said Moi aussi! when he found out he was also six. What do you think moi aussi means? When else could you use it?
Challenge
Why do you think French has two spellings for content / contente but English only has one word, “happy”? Is it more helpful, or more complicated? Explain.

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 2 · Unit 2 · Mon école

Les couleurs, les nombres et « Est-ce que je peux…? »

Colours, numbers and asking for what I need

B1.1B1.2B2.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

You need a red crayon, but you don't know the word for “red” in French. Your friend has the whole box. What could you do?

Puzzle: how many different ways can you get your message across when you're missing a word? Pointing? Acting? Describing it with other words? Which way is fastest? Which one teaches you the most?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B1.1Use speaking strategies when I don't know a word: point, gesture, show, or ask Comment dit-on…?
  • B1.2Say colours and numbers 0–10 and describe my school things (J'ai trois crayons rouges).
  • B2.2Ask for things politely and answer when someone asks me: Est-ce que je peux avoir…? Oui, voilà!

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

What your child learns

This is a vocabulary-heavy week: 11 colours, numbers 0–10, and a key request formula. The communication strategies in Part 4 are as important as the words — they give your child a way to keep talking even when they're stuck.

Teaching tips
  • Colours: use real objects everywhere. “C'est quelle couleur?” while pointing at a banana, a car, a sock. Aim for 20 quick questions a day.
  • Numbers: count everything — stairs, grapes, jumps. Count backwards from 10 as a rocket launch: dix, neuf, huit… zéro! Décollage! (Lift-off!)
  • Requests: from now on, when your child wants a snack or a toy, prompt them to ask in French. Accept any attempt.
You can say“If you don't know a French word, you have lots of tricks! You can point, you can act it out, or you can ask me: Comment dit-on ‘scissors’ en français?”
Watch for this misconceptionIn French, the colour usually comes after the thing: un crayon rouge (a pencil red). Don't teach it as a rule; just always model it that way. By Grade 2 it becomes natural.
Watch for this misconceptionSept (7) has a silent p; six and dix sound different when alone (sees, dees) than before a word (six crayons = see kreh-YO(N)). Don't worry — the speaker button handles it; your child will copy.
How you'll know it clickedYour child counts to 10 and back, names at least 8 colours correctly when you point, and asks for 3 different objects using Est-ce que je peux avoir… s'il te plaît? When stuck on a word, they use a strategy instead of switching to English.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Les couleurs (colours)

Les couleurs · Colours

rougeROOZHredbleuBLUHbluejauneZHOHNyellowvertVEHRgreenorangeo-RA(N)ZHorangeviolet / mauvevyo-LEH / MOHVpurpleroseROHZpinknoirNWARblackblancBLA(N)whitebrunBRUH(N)browngrisGREEgrey
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Canadians usually say brun for brown, while people in France usually say marron — which is also the word for a chestnut! And in Quebec and Ontario, many people say mauve for purple. Same language, different colours of words!

Part 3 · Asking and answering
To askTo answer
Est-ce que je peux avoir…, s'il te plaît?ESS-kuh zhuh puh a-VWAR… seel tuh PLEHCan I have…, please?Oui, voilà!wee, vwa-LAYes, here you go!

Part 4 · When you're missing a word

Every language learner gets stuck. Smart speakers use these strategies:

StrategyWhat it looks like
Point or showPoint to the object: Est-ce que je peux avoir… ça? (çaSAthat)
Act it outMake a cutting motion with two fingers for scissors.
Describe itC'est rouge… c'est pour couper… (It's red… it's for cutting…)
Ask for the wordComment dit-on « glue » en français?ko-MA(N) dee-TO(N) … a(n) fra(n)-SEHHow do you say “glue” in French?
Use your face and voiceSmile, look hopeful, make your voice go up for a question.
Surprising factScientists who study language learning found that learners who use gestures and keep talking — even with mistakes — learn faster than learners who stay quiet until they're perfect. Being brave is a learning strategy!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Léa said un crayon rouge. In English we say “a red pencil”. What's different about the order? Can you make another one: a blue book?
Stretch
You want the glue but forgot the word colle. Show three different ways you could still get the glue — in French.
Challenge
Why do you think the number words for 1–10 sound so different from English, but words like zéro and orange sound almost the same? Where might those words have come from?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Run a pretend school-supply store where every item must be requested in French.

Materials

  • Real school supplies in different colours
  • Small price tags (0–10 “sous”)
  • Pretend coins (buttons, 10 each)
  • A table as the store counter

Steps

  1. Set up the magasin (store) with supplies. Put a price tag from 0 to 10 on each.
  2. Child is the customer and must ask: Est-ce que je peux avoir le crayon bleu, s'il vous plaît? (vous — the store clerk is an adult!)
  3. Parent-clerk asks Combien de…? and says the price: C'est quatre sous. Child counts out coins in French.
  4. Swap roles — child runs the store and counts the money.
  5. Strategy challenge: parent hides the word list. Child must get 2 items using only strategies from Part 4.

What I asked forColourPriceStrategy I used

Assignment · Le devoir

Notebook work.

Part A — Colour and count

Draw your pencil case. Draw and colour your supplies. Say (and parent writes, child copies one): J'ai trois crayons rouges. J'ai une gomme bleue.

Part B — Number book

Make a mini-book: one page per number from 1 to 10 with that many drawings. Read it aloud in French.

Part C — Stuck? No problem!

Tell about a time this week you didn't know a word. Which strategy did you use? Did it work?

Homework · À la maison

1 · Colour I-spy

Play Je vois quelque chose de… rouge! (I spy something… red!) in the car or at dinner every day. Your child must name the colour in French.

2 · Ask in French

For the whole week, snacks and toys are requested in French: Est-ce que je peux avoir une pomme, s'il te plaît? Keep a tally of successful French requests.

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Do you think people who speak different languages see colours differently? (Some languages have no separate word for blue and green!)
  2. What would the world be like without numbers? Could you still share things fairly?
  3. Is pointing a kind of language? Could two people have a whole conversation just by pointing?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 3 · Unit 3 · Mon corps

Je parle bien: les sons, le rythme et « J'ai mal! »

Speaking smoothly: sounds, rhythm and feelings

B1.1B1.3B2.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Say this in English, three different ways: “Really.” Now: “Really?” Now: “REALLY!”

The same word meant three different things — just because your voice changed. Puzzle: if the voice can change what a word means, is speaking really about words at all? What else is your voice telling people?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B1.3Speak with a smooth pace, good pronunciation of tricky French sounds (u, r, on, an), and the right intonation for questions and exclamations.
  • B1.1Use my body, face and voice to help others understand me (gestures, expressions, volume).
  • B2.1Adjust my voice to the situation: quiet voice, talking voice, outside voice; stay on topic.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Focus: pronunciation and prosody

This week is a “speech gym”. Your child practises the French sounds that don't exist in English, and the music of French: stress falls on the last syllable, and questions rise at the end. Your pronunciation doesn't need to be perfect — use the speaker buttons as the model and be your child's practice partner.

Warm-ups (5 minutes every day)
  • The fish face for u: say “ee”, freeze your tongue, then push your lips into a tiny round “o”. Try tutüyou lunelünmoon ruerüstreet.
  • The gargle for r: pretend to gargle water very gently. Try rougeroozhred ratrarat.
  • The nose hum for nasal sounds: pinch your nose — nasal sounds will buzz! Try bonbonbo(n)-bo(n)candy mamanma-ma(n)mom.
You can say“French words like to put their strong beat at the end: ba-na-NE, not BA-na-na. Let's clap the beat: cho-co-LAT!”
Watch for this misconceptionChildren (and parents) often stress the first syllable, English-style: “CHO-co-lat”. Clap the syllables and make the last clap loudest.
Useful for real lifeHealth vocabulary (Part 3) is practical: if your child ever attends a French school or camp, J'ai mal à… is how they'll tell an adult they're hurt. Practise it seriously once, then play the doctor game.
How you'll know it clickedYour child can say the 3 “speech gym” sounds recognisably, raise their voice at the end of a question, tell you where it hurts using J'ai mal à…, and switch between quiet, talking and outside voices on request.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · The music of French

Clap the syllables and make the last clap BIG. Then say the word with the speaker.

WordClap itEnglish cousin (stress at the start!)

Part 2 · Questions go UP, answers go DOWN

In French you can turn a sentence into a question just by making your voice go up at the end! Listen, then copy.

Statement (voice goes down ↘)Question (voice goes up ↗)
Tu as mal.tü a MALYou're hurt.Tu as mal?tü a MAL ↗Are you hurt?
Ça va.sa VAIt's okay.Ça va?sa VA ↗Is it okay?
C'est bon.seh BO(N)It's good.C'est bon?seh BO(N) ↗Is it good?
Il fait froid.eel feh FRWAIt's cold.Il fait froid?eel feh FRWA ↗Is it cold?
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?In English, you usually need extra words for a question (“Do you…?”, “Is it…?”). In spoken French, your voice alone can do the job. Your voice is a question mark!
Part 3 · Aïe! J'ai mal! (Ouch! It hurts!)

When you're hurt, you need to tell someone. In French you say J'ai mal à… and the body part.

Chez le médecin · At the doctor's

Part 4 · Three voices

Good speakers change their voice for the place they're in. Practise saying Bonjour!bo(n)-ZHOORHello! in all three voices:

VoiceWhenSay it like…
la voix chuchotéela vwa shü-sho-TAYthe whisper voiceLibrary, when the baby sleeps, secretsa whisper
la voix normalela vwa nor-MALthe talking voiceConversations, the classroom, the tablenormal
la voix fortela vwa FORTthe outside voicePlayground, calling someone far away, singing on stageloud (but not screaming!)
Surprising factDid you know your voice comes from two tiny folds in your throat — the vocal cords — that vibrate hundreds of times every second when you talk? Put your hand on your throat and say Ahhh: you can feel them buzzing! When you whisper, they don't vibrate at all.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Say Ça va and Ça va? Which one is a question? What did your voice do differently?
Stretch
Why do you think French and English put the strong beat in different places in the same word (cho-co-LAT vs CHOC-o-late)?
Challenge
Imagine you're in a French school, you're hurt, and the teacher is busy. Plan exactly what you'd do and say — your body, your voice, your words. Act it out.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Play doctor's office with correct pronunciation, question intonation and appropriate voices.

Materials

  • Toy doctor kit (or a spoon as a thermometer, a cup as a stethoscope)
  • Bandages or strips of paper
  • Stuffed animal patients
  • A mirror

Steps

  1. Speech gym (5 min): in front of a mirror, practise the fish face (u), the gargle (r) and the nose hum (on/an).
  2. Child is le docteur / la docteure. Stuffed animals are patients. Parent voices the patients: J'ai mal au ventre! Child puts a bandage on the right place.
  3. Swap: child is the patient and must say where it hurts with the right body part.
  4. The doctor asks questions with rising voice: Tu as mal? Ça va? Parent checks the voice goes up.
  5. Voice game: say the same sentence in whisper, talking and outside voice. Parent names a place (library! playground!); child picks the voice.

Notebook and speaking assignment.

Part A — Poor Teddy!

Draw a teddy bear with 4 bandages. For each one, say out loud J'ai mal à… and parent writes the sentence; child copies one.

Part B — My sound report card

Try each tricky sound: tu, rouge, bonbon, maman. Colour a star for each one you're proud of. Which sound needs more practice?

Part C — Voice rules

Draw three places (library, table, playground). For each, write which voice you use and why.

1 · Tongue twister of the week

Practise one French tongue twister (virelangue) every day and perform it on Friday: Un chasseur sachant chasser sait chasser sans son chien.uh(n) sha-SUHR sa-sha(n) sha-SAY seh sha-SAY sa(n) so(n) SHYA(N)A hunter who knows how to hunt can hunt without his dog. Start with the Slow voice!

2 · Feelings at dinner

Each night at dinner, everyone says one feeling sentence and one J'ai mal à… or Je n'ai pas mal! (Nothing hurts!).

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Why can you recognise your mom's or dad's voice on the phone without seeing them? What makes every voice different?
  2. Parrots can say French words. Do they speak French? What's the difference between saying words and speaking?
  3. Could you invent a language that uses only music, with no words?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 4 · Unit 4 · Ma famille, ma maison

Voici ma famille! Ma présentation

My family show-and-tell: a presentation

B1.2B1.4B2.3
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

TV presenters, YouTubers and news reporters practise what they're going to say — sometimes dozens of times — before the camera turns on. Then they make it look easy!

Puzzle: if you were making a mini-show about your family, what would you show? What would you say? And how many times would you need to practise before it felt easy?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B1.2Present my family and my home in French using practised sentences (Voici mon frère. Il s'appelle… Il a… ans.).
  • B1.4Create an oral media text: a photo slideshow, a drawing show or a short video with my voice describing my family.
  • B2.3(a) Describe the strategies that helped me prepare and speak; (b) name what I did well and one thing to improve next time.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The project

Your child creates their first media presentation: a “show” about their family, using photos or drawings, which they narrate in French. It can be a phone slideshow with voice-over, a paper “TV” (a box with a scroll of drawings), or a simple video. Keep it short: 5–8 sentences.

Steps across the week
  1. Mon–Tue: learn family and home words; practise the sentence patterns.
  2. Wed: plan the show (choose 4–6 pictures, one sentence each).
  3. Thu: rehearse 3 times with feedback; record the final version.
  4. Fri: watch it together, celebrate, and do the self-reflection (B2.3).
You can say“A great presenter looks at the audience, speaks slowly, and smiles. Let's practise like real TV hosts!”
Grammar in a sentenceUse il (he) for boys/men and elle (she) for girls/women: Voici ma sœur. Elle s'appelle Maya. Elle a quatre ans. For pets, use il or elle depending on the animal's name/sex — French has no “it” for animals.
Watch for this misconceptionmon / ma / mes (my) change with the word: mon père, ma mère, mes grands-parents. Don't lecture; the sentence frames below already have the right one. Just copy the model.
How you'll know it clickedYour child presents 5+ sentences about their family, mostly without prompting, while looking at the audience; can describe one thing they did to prepare (“I practised with the pictures”) and one thing to improve.

Part 3 · How to be a great presenter
Presenter tipWhy it works
Look at your audience (Regarde ton public)People listen better when you look at them.
Point to your picture as you talkPictures help listeners understand French words.
Slow down and pause after each sentenceYour listeners need time to think.
Smile and use your talking voiceYour voice shows you're proud of your family!
End with Merci!mehr-SEEThank you!It tells everyone you're done — time to clap!
Real-life presenterSome of the most famous presenters in the French-speaking world started small. Michaëlle Jean was born in Haiti, moved to Quebec as a child, became a TV journalist on Radio-Canada, and later became Governor General of Canada (2005–2010) and then the leader of the whole international Francophonie organisation. She speaks five languages!
Part 4 · Media: what makes a good family show?

Think about videos you've watched. What makes a video fun to watch? Music? Close-up pictures? Funny moments? Choose one special effect for your show — a sound, a surprise picture, a costume, or a “ta-da!” moment.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Léa said Il s'appelle for her dad and Elle s'appelle for her mom. Which one would you use for your grandma? For your uncle? For your dog named Luna?
Stretch
What's the difference between talking to your family at dinner and presenting to them? What changes — your voice, your body, your words?
Challenge
Pictures help listeners understand. If your show was on the radio (no pictures), what would you need to add or change so people could still understand?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Plan, rehearse and record a family media presentation.

Materials

  • Family photos (printed or on a phone) or drawings
  • A shoebox “TV” with a paper scroll (optional)
  • Phone or tablet for recording
  • The planning table below

Steps

  1. Choose 4–6 pictures: family members, a pet, your home or favourite room.
  2. For each picture, choose one sentence frame from Part 1 and fill it in. Write it in the planning table.
  3. Rehearsal 1: say each sentence while holding the picture. Parent gives one “star” (something good) and one “wish” (something to improve).
  4. Rehearsal 2 and 3: improve the wish. Add your special effect.
  5. Record the final show (slideshow with voice, or video). Watch it together!

Part A — Storyboard

Draw your show as a comic strip, one box per picture. Under each box, copy your sentence.

Part B — Stars and wishes

Answer: What did I do well in my show? (2 stars) What will I do better next time? (1 wish)

Part C — My preparation

Homework · À la maison

1 · World premiere

Show your family presentation to someone outside your home (a grandparent on video, a neighbour, a friend). Ask them one question in French afterwards: Tu as aimé? (Did you like it?)

2 · House tour

Give a French house tour to a stuffed animal: Voici la cuisine! Voici ma chambre! Every room you enter this week — name it in French.

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. What makes a family a family? Is it being related, living together, loving each other — or something else?
  2. If your home could talk, what would it say about your family?
  3. Why do we feel nervous when we talk in front of people, even people we love? What does nervous feel like in your body?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 5 · Unit 5 · L'hiver

Qu'est-ce que je porte? On parle de l'hiver

What am I wearing? Winter talk and the Carnaval

B1.3B2.2B3.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Canadian children put on more clothes in winter than almost any children on Earth: snow pants, boots, coat, scarf, tuque, mittens… Some families call it the winter armour.

Puzzle: could you describe exactly what you're wearing so clearly — in French — that someone with their eyes closed could draw you? What would you need to say first?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B1.3Speak smoothly and clearly about what I'm wearing, using practised sentences (Je porte une tuque rouge).
  • B2.2Take part in guessing games and short spontaneous conversations about clothes and winter activities.
  • B3.1Talk about winter traditions in French-speaking communities (Carnaval de Québec, Bonhomme, winter festivals in Ontario) and connect them to my own winter.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

This week

Your child moves from single words to full sentences with a colour: Je porte un manteau bleu. They also start spontaneous speaking — answering unplanned questions in games. Expect mistakes; that's how spontaneous speech develops.

Tips
  • Get dressed for outdoor play in French every day: Mets ta tuque! Où sont tes mitaines? (Put on your hat! Where are your mittens?)
  • Play Qui est-ce? (Guess who) with family members' clothes.
  • Talk about Carnaval (Part 4) with photos or videos if you can find them (search “Carnaval de Québec”).
You can say“Let's describe what we're wearing like fashion reporters! Aujourd'hui, je porte un chandail vert! Now you!”
Watch for this misconceptionColours that end in -e (rouge, jaune, rose, orange) are the same for boy- and girl-words. Others add -e for girl-words: un manteau vert / une tuque verte (you can hear the t!). Model it; don't drill it.
How you'll know it clickedYour child can describe 3 pieces of clothing with colours in full sentences, ask and answer Qu'est-ce que tu portes? in a game, and tell you 2 facts about the Carnaval de Québec.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Les vêtements (clothes)

Les vêtements · Clothes

un chandailuh(n) sha(n)-DYEa sweaterun t-shirtuh(n) tee-SHURTa t-shirtun pantalonuh(n) pa(n)-ta-LO(N)pantsune robeün ROBa dressune jupeün ZHÜPa skirtdes basday BAsocks (Canadian)des souliersday soo-LYAYshoes (Canadian)un manteauuh(n) ma(n)-TOHa coatune tuqueün TÜKa winter hatdes mitainesday mee-TEHNmittensun foularduh(n) foo-LARa scarfdes bottesday BUTboots
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Canadian French uses some words that are different from France: chandail (France: pull), bas (France: chaussettes), souliers (France: chaussures), tuque (France: bonnet), mitaines (France: moufles). If you visit France, people will still understand you!
Part 2 · Je porte… (I'm wearing…)
Part 3 · Winter fun — what do you like to do?
faire un bonhomme de neigefehr uh(n) bo-NUM duh NEHZHbuild a snowmanglisserglee-SAYgo sledding / slidingpatinerpa-tee-NAYskatejouer au hockeyzhoo-AY oh o-KEHplay hockeyfaire des anges dans la neigefehr day-ZA(N)ZH da(n) la NEHZHmake snow angelsboire un chocolat chaudbwar uh(n) sho-ko-la SHOHdrink hot chocolate

Say what you like: En hiver, j'aime glisser!a(n)-nee-VEHR, zhehm glee-SAYIn winter, I like sledding!

Part 4 · Le Carnaval de Québec and winter in Ontario

Remember Bonhomme Carnaval from the listening lesson? Now you can talk about him! Bonhomme porte une tuque rouge et une ceinture fléchée.bo-NUM port ün TÜK roozh ay ün sa(n)-TÜR flay-SHAYBonhomme wears a red winter hat and an arrow sash.

The ceinture fléchée (arrow sash) is a long, colourful woven belt with arrow patterns. It was worn by voyageurs — French-Canadian and Métis canoe travellers who paddled across Canada 300 years ago — to keep warm and protect their backs. Today it's a symbol of French-Canadian and Métis culture.

Ontario has winter festivals too! Many francophone communities hold carnavals d'hiver with snow sculptures, sugar-shack food, fiddle music and outdoor games. In Ottawa, Winterlude / Bal de Neige takes place on the Rideau Canal, which becomes one of the longest skating rinks in the world!

Surprising factThe Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa is about 7.8 km long when it's fully open — the length of about 130 hockey rinks in a row. Some people skate to work on it!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
What's the difference between Je porte and Tu portes? Who is wearing the clothes in each one?
Stretch
Why do you think voyageurs wore a sash instead of a normal belt? Think about paddling a canoe all day in the cold.
Challenge
If a child from Senegal (where it's hot all year) visited you in January, what would you tell them to wear? Plan a French conversation with them.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Play clothing guessing games and speak spontaneously about winter.

Materials

  • A pile of family winter clothes
  • Blindfold (scarf)
  • Dice
  • Hot chocolate for the end!

Steps

  1. Fashion show: child puts on layers of winter clothes, walking the “runway” and announcing each one: Je porte une tuque bleue!
  2. Qui est-ce? Parent describes a family member's clothes: Il porte un chandail gris… Child guesses who. Then swap.
  3. Blindfold game: child is blindfolded; parent hands them a piece of clothing. Child feels it and guesses: C'est une mitaine!
  4. Dice talk: roll the die. 1 = say what you're wearing, 2 = a winter activity you like, 3 = ask a question, 4 = say something about Bonhomme, 5 = describe the weather, 6 = free choice!
  5. Celebrate with hot chocolate — ordered in French!

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  2. Snowmen exist all over the world where it snows. Who do you think made the very first one?
  3. Voyageurs travelled thousands of kilometres by canoe. What would you need to bring — and to know how to say — on a trip like that?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 6 · Unit 6 · Miam!

J'aime, j'adore, je n'aime pas: on parle de nourriture

I like, I love, I don't like: talking about food

B2.1B2.2B3.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Someone offers you a food you really, really don't like. In English you might say “Ew, gross!” — but that could hurt the cook's feelings.

Puzzle: how can you tell someone the truth (you don't like it) and be kind at the same time? Are there polite ways to say no in every language? Let's find the French ones.

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B2.2Have a conversation about food: ask and answer Tu aimes…? J'aime / J'adore / Je n'aime pas / Je déteste…
  • B2.1Show good conversation behaviour: take turns, stay on topic, and respond to what my partner says (Moi aussi! Pas moi!).
  • B3.2Use polite table and restaurant expressions: Bon appétit, S'il vous plaît, Non, merci, C'est délicieux.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Why this matters

Opinions are the engine of real conversation. Once your child can say J'aime / Je n'aime pas, they can talk about anything! This week also builds responding to a partner (Moi aussi / Pas moi), which turns two monologues into a real exchange.

The opinion scale

Make a big arrow on paper from 😍 to 🤢 (or from a heart to a thumbs-down) and place the four expressions on it. Use it all week.

You can say“In French we have four levels of liking: j'adore (I love), j'aime (I like), je n'aime pas (I don't like), je déteste (I hate). But at someone's table, the kind thing is Non, merci.”
Watch for this misconceptionAfter j'aime / j'adore / je déteste, French uses le / la / les: J'aime les pommes. J'adore le chocolat. English says “I like apples” without “the”. Model with the article every time; the frames below do it for you.
Family habitBon appétit! is said before every meal in French-speaking homes — try it at every family meal this month. It's a lovely habit.
How you'll know it clickedYour child holds a 6-turn conversation about food, using at least three of the four opinion levels and responding to you with Moi aussi / Pas moi. At the table, they say Bon appétit and Non, merci politely.

Part 4 · Polite at the table

À table · At the table

Bon appétit!bo(n)-na-pay-TEEEnjoy your meal!C'est délicieux!seh day-lee-SYUHIt's delicious!Encore, s'il te plaît!a(n)-KOR, seel tuh PLEHMore, please!Non, merci.no(n), mehr-SEENo, thank you.J'ai faim!zhay FA(N)I'm hungry!J'ai soif!zhay SWAFI'm thirsty!Je n'ai plus faim, merci.zhuh neh plü FA(N), mehr-SEEI'm full, thank you.Est-ce que je peux sortir de table?ESS-kuh zhuh puh sor-TEER duh TABLMay I leave the table?
Surprising factPoutine — fries, cheese curds and gravy — was invented in rural Quebec in the 1950s. Several towns claim they invented it first! Real poutine cheese curds should squeak against your teeth when they're fresh. French speakers call them fromage en grains or fromage qui fait couic-couic (squeaky cheese)!

Honest and kind: at someone's home, if you don't like a food, the polite answer is Non, merci.no(n), mehr-SEENo, thank you. — not Je déteste ça! Save je déteste for games and conversations with friends.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Noah said Moi aussi! and Léa said Pas moi! When would you use each one? Give an example with a food you love.
Stretch
Why is Non, merci kinder than Je déteste ça at your friend's house, even though both are honest?
Challenge
“I like apples” in French is J'aime les pommes — it has an extra “the”. Why might French need that little word when English doesn't? Is French talking about these apples or all apples?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Run a family taste test and hold opinion conversations in French.

Materials

  • 5–6 small foods to taste (fruit, cheese, cracker, vegetable, a surprise one)
  • Opinion scale arrow on paper
  • Blindfold (optional)

Steps

  1. Place foods on a plate. Name each one in French together.
  2. Taste test: child tastes each food (blindfolded for fun, if they like) and places it on the opinion scale while saying the sentence: J'adore le fromage!
  3. Parent does the same. After each of your opinions, child responds: Moi aussi! / Pas moi! / Moi non plus!
  4. Survey: child interviews 3 family members or toys: Tu aimes les carottes? and records answers.
  5. Close the session with polite table talk: C'est délicieux! Merci!

Part B — Survey results

Draw a simple picture graph of your survey. Which food was the most popular? Say it in French: Tout le monde aime… (Everybody likes…)

Part C — Good conversation rules

Answer: What makes a conversation good? (taking turns, staying on topic, answering the other person…) Which one do you do best?

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 7 · Unit 7 · Les animaux

Devine mon animal! Je décris et je présente

Guess my animal! Describing and performing

B1.1B1.2B1.4
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

A riddle: “I'm grey. I'm very, very big. I have big ears and a long nose. I live in Africa.” — You guessed it before the end, didn't you?

Puzzle: which clue gave it away? Which clues were useless? If you want someone to guess your animal fast, which clue should you give first — and which should you save for last to make it fun?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B1.2Describe an animal in French: its colour, size, body parts, where it lives and what it eats (Il est gris. Il a…).
  • B1.1Use strategies to make my description clear: gestures, sounds, drawings, and choosing the best clues.
  • B1.4Create an oral media text: a recorded riddle show or puppet show about animals.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Focus: descriptive speaking

Riddles (devinettes) are perfect for Grade 1: they're short, repeatable, and require clear description. By the end of the week your child records a “Devinettes” video show with 3–4 animal riddles.

Tips
  • Start with the riddle frame (Part 2) and practise it with 5–6 animals.
  • Talk about clue order: easy clues first make it too quick; tricky clues first make it fun!
  • Encourage acting and sounds as strategies (B1.1).
You can say“A good riddle-maker is like a magician: give little clues first, and save the best clue for the end!”
Watch for this misconceptionIl est (he is) is followed by a describing word (Il est gros); Il a (he has) is followed by a thing (Il a une queue). Mixing them (Il est une queue) is very common. Recast: “Il a une queue!”
How you'll know it clickedYour child creates and performs 3 riddles of 4+ clues each, mostly independently, and uses at least one strategy (gesture or sound) when a word is missing. The recorded show is complete.

Surprising factThe Arctic fox changes colour: its fur is white in winter to hide in the snow and brown or grey in summer to hide among rocks. It's a riddle all by itself — Je suis blanc… ou brun?
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Canada's national animal is the beaver (le castor). Canada also has more polar bears (ours polaires) than any other country — about two thirds of all polar bears in the world live in Canada!

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 8 · Unit 8 · Le calendrier et la météo

Je suis météorologue! Et mes objectifs en parlant

The weather reporter and my speaking goals

B1.3B2.2B2.3
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

A weather reporter speaks for about 90 seconds without notes, looking at a camera, pointing at a map nobody else can see (it's a green screen!). They make it look easy.

Puzzle: how do they remember everything? What tricks might they use so they don't get lost in the middle? Could you do a 30-second weather report in French?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B1.3Speak smoothly and confidently in a planned weather report: the date, the day, the weather and what to wear.
  • B2.2Answer spontaneous questions about the date, weather and seasons (Quel temps fait-il? Quelle est la date?).
  • B2.3(a) Describe strategies that help me speak well; (b) name my speaking strengths and set a speaking goal with steps.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

This week

Your child has been doing the morning ritual for months — now they perform it as a weather report, adding seasons and numbers up to 31. The week ends with a speaking self-assessment and goal-setting session (metacognition).

Tips
  • Make a “green screen” — a big blue or green paper map of Ontario on the wall.
  • Practise numbers 11–31 through the calendar (Part 2) — count days of the month together.
  • Compare with a video from the start of the year if you have one.
You can say“Real weather reporters use three tricks: they plan the order, they use the map to remind them, and they practise. Let's use all three!”
Watch for this misconceptionNumbers 11–16 are special words (onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize). From 17 on, it's logical: dix-sept = ten-seven! Point out the pattern; children love finding it.
How you'll know it clickedYour child gives a 30-second weather report fluently (few long pauses), answers 3 unplanned questions about date/weather, and states a speaking goal they chose themselves.

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Notice: you say au printemps but en été, en automne, en hiver. Why? Because été, automne, hiver start with a vowel sound (h is silent!) and en slides into them more smoothly. French loves smooth sounds!

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Perform a weather report and answer surprise questions, then self-assess.

Materials

  • Big paper map of Ontario (or a world map)
  • Weather symbol cards from Unit 5
  • A pointer (a wooden spoon)
  • Phone to record

Steps

  1. Plan the report in order: greeting → day and date → season → weather in 2 cities → tomorrow → goodbye.
  2. Stick weather cards on the map. Rehearse with the pointer twice.
  3. Perform and record. Parent is the “news anchor” and asks 2 surprise questions afterward: Quel temps fait-il à Toronto? Qu'est-ce qu'on porte?
  4. Watch the recording. Child fills in the strategy checklist (Part 4) honestly.
  5. Compare with an older recording (Unit 1 intro). What changed?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Parler · Speaking — Lesson 9 · Unit 9 · Ma communauté, notre francophonie

Fier / fière de parler français: ma communauté

Proud to speak French: my community presentation

B3.1B1.2B1.4B2.3
1–2 weeks · 5–8 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

A hundred years ago in Ontario, there was a law called Regulation 17 that made it very hard for children to learn in French at school. Families and teachers protested for 15 years — some teachers even taught in secret — until the law was dropped in 1927.

Puzzle: why would people fight so hard for their children to learn in their language? What is a language worth? What would you do if someone said you couldn't speak your language at school?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • B3.1Talk about French-speaking communities in Ontario — their places, symbols, celebrations, people and contributions — and connect them to my own experience.
  • B1.2Present information about my community (places, helpers, what I like) using practised sentences.
  • B1.4Create an oral media text: a mini-documentary, guided tour video or podcast about francophone Ontario or my community.
  • B2.3Look back on my year of speaking: my best strategies, my progress, my goals for Grade 2.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The final speaking project

Your child creates a short mini-documentary (video, slideshow with voice, or “podcast” audio) about francophone Ontario and their own community: 8–10 sentences. It connects everything from the year: introductions, descriptions, opinions and culture.

About Regulation 17 (for you)

Regulation 17 (1912–1927) restricted French-language instruction in Ontario schools to the first two grades. Franco-Ontarian families resisted strongly; a famous example is the teachers of the École Guigues in Ottawa, where mothers guarded the school with hatpins to keep inspectors out, and teacher Jeanne Lajoie in Pembroke, who taught French in a private school after being dismissed. You can share the story simply: “Some people once tried to stop children learning in French, and families bravely stood up for their language.”

You can say“French is a language that Franco-Ontarians fought to keep. When you speak French, you're part of that story too!”
How you'll know it clickedYour child presents 8+ sentences about places, helpers and francophone culture in Ontario, including at least 2 facts about Franco-Ontarians, and reflects on their year: one strategy, one area of pride, one goal.

Part 3 · Francophone Ontario — what I can tell people
Surprising factFrench speakers have been in what is now Ontario for about 400 years. In 1615, French explorer Samuel de Champlain travelled to the Georgian Bay area, and one of the oldest European settlements in Ontario was a French mission called Sainte-Marie among the Hurons (near Midland), built in 1639 near the Wendat (Huron) people. Today there's a reconstructed village you can visit!
Part 4 · Franco-Ontarian people to know
PersonWhy they matter
Gaétan Gervais & Michel DupuisCreated the Franco-Ontarian flag in Sudbury in 1975.
Jeanne LajoieA young teacher in Pembroke who kept teaching in French during Regulation 17. Several schools are named after her.
Paul DemersSinger who co-wrote Notre place, the official Franco-Ontarian anthem.
Michaëlle JeanHaitian-born journalist; Governor General of Canada and head of the international Francophonie.
Your local francophones!Ask: who speaks French in your neighbourhood, school or family?

Lessons · Leçons

Lire · Reading — Lesson 1 · Unit 1 · Bonjour!

L'alphabet, mon nom et les cartes de souhaits

Letters, names and greeting cards

C1.1C1.2C3.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

French and English use the same 26 letters. But French letters wear little hats and tails: é, è, ê, à, ç, ô, ï…

Puzzle: why would a language put hats on its letters? What job could a tiny mark above a letter possibly do? Look at é and e — do you think they sound the same? How could you find out?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C1.1Use reading strategies before, during and after reading: look at pictures, find letters and words I know, and point to each word as I read.
  • C1.2Understand short greeting cards and name labels with familiar words and pictures.
  • C3.2Find examples of friendly and polite greetings in written French (Salut, Chère Madame, Bonjour).

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

How children learn to read in French

Your child is learning to read in two languages that share an alphabet but not always the same sounds. That's normal and fine: research shows reading skills transfer between languages. This year we build: (1) the French alphabet names and vowel sounds, (2) one sound of the week per lesson, (3) sight words (mots fréquents) read instantly, and (4) short patterned texts.

This week
  1. Sing/say the alphabet with the speaker (Part 1). Point to each letter.
  2. Learn the 5 vowel sounds. They are short and pure in French — no English “glide”.
  3. Read the name cards and greeting cards together. Your child points to each word as it is read (“finger tracking”).
You can say“Reading is like being a detective too! First we look at the pictures for clues. Then we look for letters and words we know. And we always point to the words as we read.”
Watch for this misconceptionFrench letter names differ from English: e is “uh”, i is “ee”, j is “zhee”, g is “zhay”, r is “ehr”, u is “ü”, w is “doo-bluh-vay” (double v!), y is “ee-grek” (Greek i!). Use the speaker button; don't rely on memory.
How you'll know it clickedYour child can name most letters in French, read their own name and 4 sight words by sight, and point to the word Bonjour or Salut on a card and tell you who the card is for (friend or adult).

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · L'alphabet français
Did you know? · Le savais-tu?In French, Y is called i grec — “Greek I” — because it came from the Greek alphabet. And W is double vé — “double V” — while in English it's “double U”. Look at it: is it two Vs or two Us?
Part 2 · Les voyelles (vowels) — the singing letters

Les voyelles · Vowels

a — amiaha as in ami (friend)e — leuhe as in le (the)i — liteei as in lit (bed)o — motooho as in moto (motorbike)u — tuü (ee with round lips)u as in tu (you)é — étéayé as in été (summer)

The little mark on é is called an accent aigu (sharp accent). It changes the sound from “uh” to “ay”. So yes — hats change sounds!

Mots fréquents · Sight words (learn to read these by sight)

jezhuhIsuissweeametayandouiweeyesnonno(n)nobonjourbo(n)-zhoorhello
Part 3 · Read the name cards

Before reading: look at the pictures (imagine a boy, a girl, a teacher). During: point to each word. After: Who is who?

Part 4 · Greeting cards — who are they for?

Read each card. Look for the greeting word. Is the card for a friend or for an adult?

Card 1 says Salut — friendly, for a friend. Card 2 says Chère Madame — polite, for a teacher. Card 3 says Bisous (kisses) — very friendly, for family. Words tell you who a card is for!

Surprising factLouis Braille, a French boy who became blind at age 3, invented the braille alphabet — letters made of raised dots you read with your fingers — when he was only 15 years old, in 1824. Today blind people all over the world read with his invention. A teenager changed reading forever!

Challenge

  2. Put the cards in order on the floor. Jump from letter to letter saying the names!

  4. Sight word hunt: hide the 6 sight words (on sticky notes) around the room. Child finds and reads each one.

Lire · Reading — Lesson 2 · Unit 2 · Mon école

Les mots amis et les étiquettes de la classe

Word friends: cognates and classroom labels

C1.3C1.4C2.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

You already know hundreds of French words — and you've never studied them! Piano. Orange. Animal. Chocolat. Table. Zéro. Bébé. Ballon.

Puzzle: how is that possible? Why would two different languages share so many words? And can you trust every word that looks like English… or are there tricks?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C1.4Use strategies to grow my vocabulary while reading: spot cognates (mots amis) and words I already know.
  • C1.3Read labels and short classroom sentences smoothly, with growing speed (C'est un crayon. Voici la table.).
  • C2.1Explain why labels, lists and signs are written (to name things, to remember, to give instructions).

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Cognates are your child's superpower

About a third of English words came from French (after the Norman conquest of England in 1066, French was spoken at the English royal court for centuries). That means many French words look like English. These are called cognates or, in French, mots amis (friend words). Teaching your child to spot them is one of the fastest ways to grow reading vocabulary.

But beware the “faux amis”!

Some words look the same but mean something different: faux amis (false friends). Example: librairie = bookstore (not library!); crayon = pencil; chair = flesh (not chair!). Make it a fun “trap” game.

You can say“Let's go hunting for mots amis — French words that look like English. But careful: some are sneaky tricksters!”
PhonicsSound of the week: “ou” — two letters together make one sound, “oo”. This is your child's first letter team. Point out: o + u = ou.
How you'll know it clickedYour child identifies at least 10 cognates in a text, reads the classroom label sentences with smooth finger-tracking, and explains what a label is for.

Surprising factAfter 1066, when William the Conqueror (a French-speaking duke from Normandy) became King of England, French was spoken by English kings and nobles for about 300 years. That's why so many English words come from French: table, chair, beef, pork, royal, government, restaurant… When you read French, you're reading English's cousin!

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Label your home like a French classroom and play a cognate sorting game.

Materials

  • Sticky notes or index cards
  • Tape
  • Marker
  • Two bowls labelled AMIS and FAUX AMIS

Steps

  1. Write 10 labels together: la porte, la fenêtre, la table, la chaise, le lit, le frigo, la lampe, le sofa, la télé, le livre. Child sticks each on the right object.
  2. Label tour: child walks around reading each label with the sentence C'est… / Voici…
  3. Cognate sort: parent writes 12 words on cards (8 real cognates, 4 faux amis). Child reads each and guesses friend or trickster, then checks with the speaker/English.
  4. “ou” hunt: find every “ou” in the labels and lesson — underline them.
  5. Timed reading: read the 7 classroom labels. Time it Monday and Friday. Faster?

Lire · Reading — Lesson 3 · Unit 3 · Mon corps

J'imagine! Les livres à motifs

Picture it! Pattern books and making movies in my mind

C1.1C1.2C2.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Close your eyes. Imagine a monster with three purple eyes, ten tiny arms and a nose like a carrot.

You just saw something that doesn't exist — using only words! Puzzle: how do words turn into pictures inside your head? Can you do it in French too, even with words you're still learning?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C1.1Use visualisation (making a movie in my mind) to understand what I read.
  • C1.2Understand a patterned text about the body with familiar words and pictures.
  • C2.2Notice what makes a pattern book work — repetition, rhyme, a surprise ending — and explain how it helps me read.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Visualisation and pattern books

Proficient readers make mental images as they read. We'll teach it explicitly: read a sentence, close eyes, “see” it, draw it. Pattern books (where one sentence frame repeats with one word changing) are the bread and butter of Grade 1 reading because children can predict and read them independently.

Steps
  1. Sound of the week: on (nasal). Hum it through the nose.
  2. Read the pattern book together: parent reads line 1, child reads the rest by following the pattern.
  3. Stop after each page: “Close your eyes. What do you see?”
You can say“Readers make movies in their heads. Let's read this line, then close our eyes and watch the movie. Tell me what you see!”
Early readingLet your child read the pattern book to you even if they are partly remembering rather than decoding. That's a normal first stage of reading (“emergent reading”). Then ask them to point to specific words: “Show me yeux.”
How you'll know it clickedYour child reads the pattern book aloud with finger-tracking, describes their mental images in detail, and explains that the repeating pattern helps them read the next page.

The Lesson · La leçon

Le son de la semaine · Sound of the week: on

o + n = nasal “oh”. Send the sound through your nose and don't close your lips for the n. Also spelled om before b or p.

bonbonbo(n)-bo(n)candymonmo(n)myballonba-LO(N)ballmaisonmeh-ZO(N)housecochonko-SHO(N)pignomno(n)name

Mots fréquents · Sight words (learn to read these by sight)

j'aizhayI haveaahasmonmo(n)my (masc.)mamamy (fem.)mesmaymy (plural)deuxduhtwo
Part 1 · Pattern book: Mon corps

Read it together. After each line, close your eyes and see it!

What was the pattern? Every page starts with J'ai… and then changes one thing. And the last page has a surprise: a big heart — that's about love, not just the body part!

Part 2 · Pattern book 2: Le monstre

This time, you read it. Remember to make the movie in your head!

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Avoir peur means “to be scared”, but word-for-word it's “to have fear”. French has feelings: j'ai peur (I'm scared), j'ai faim (I'm hungry), j'ai froid (I'm cold). English is feelings. Two different ways of seeing the world!
Part 3 · What makes a pattern book work?
ElementWhat it doesExample
Repetition (répétition)The same words come back, so you can predict and read them.J'ai… J'ai… J'ai…
Pictures (illustrations)Show the new word on each page.A drawing of two eyes
CountingNumbers grow page by page.trois… quatre… cinq…
Surprise endingThe pattern breaks to make you laugh or think.…peur de moi!
Surprising factYour brain has a special area that becomes a “letterbox” as you learn to read. Scientists call it the visual word form area. It's the same place in the brain for readers of French, English, Chinese or Arabic — and it gets stronger every time you read!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up

Stretch

Challenge

Objective: Make and read your own pattern book about a monster.

Materials

Steps

  1. Read both pattern books twice, finger-tracking.
  2. Visualisation drawing: parent reads 3 monster lines; child closes eyes, then draws exactly what they visualised.
  3. Make your own book: cover = Mon monstre + your name. Each page = Mon monstre a… + a number + a body part. Child copies the frame; parent helps with new words.
  4. Last page: your surprise ending!
  5. Read your book to 2 people.

Lire · Reading — Lesson 4 · Unit 4 · Ma famille, ma maison

Les livres de famille et les invitations

Family books and invitations: reading for a purpose

C1.3C2.1C3.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

A piece of paper arrives in the mail with your name on it. Before you read a single word, you already know it's an invitation to a party. How?

Puzzle: how do different kinds of writing — invitations, stories, recipes, lists — look different on the page? Could you tell what kind of text something is from across the room, without reading it?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C1.3Read a short family text aloud smoothly, with expression and growing speed.
  • C2.1Identify the purpose of different texts: a story (to enjoy), an invitation (to invite), a family book (to share information).
  • C3.1Read about Franco-Ontarian and francophone family traditions and connect them to my family.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Reading fluency

Fluency means reading smoothly, at a comfortable speed, with expression — like talking. Build it with repeated reading: read the same short text 3–4 times over the week. Each time it becomes smoother. Also use echo reading (you read a line, child echoes) and choral reading (read together).

Sound of the week: ch

c + h = “sh”, as in chat. (Not “tch” as in English “chair”!)

You can say“Let's read it like we're talking, not like a robot. Listen to how the speaker button does it, then you try!”
Watch for this misconceptionIn French, -ent at the end of verbs is silent: ils parlent = “eel PARL”. If you come across it, tell your child it's a “silent tail”.
How you'll know it clickedYour child reads the family text with only a few pauses, identifies an invitation vs. a story vs. a family book, and names one francophone family tradition from the reading.

c + h = “sh”, like the sound you make to say Chut!

Part 1 · A family book: La famille de Samuel
Part 2 · An invitation

Before reading: look at the shape of this text. It's short, with a date, a time and a place. What kind of text is it?

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?In French-speaking places, time is often written on a 24-hour clock: 14 h means 2 p.m. (12 + 2). And the “h” stands for heures (hours). Canadian trains, airports and TV schedules use it too!
Part 3 · What kind of text is it?
Text typePurposeClues on the page
Une histoire (story)To entertainTitle, characters, pictures, a beginning, middle and end
Une invitationTo invite someone to an eventQuand? Où? date, time, address, a name at the top
Un livre de familleTo share information about peopleNames, photos, Voici…
Une carte de souhaits (greeting card)To wish someone wellBonne fête! Joyeux Noël!
Part 4 · Reading about francophone families
Surprising factThiéboudienne (cheb-oo-JEN), Senegal's national dish of fish, rice and vegetables, was added to UNESCO's list of the world's intangible cultural heritage in 2021 — the same year as Haiti's soup joumou!

  2. Choral read it together, then child reads alone. Time the solo reading.
  3. Text sort: lay out real texts from home. Child sorts them by purpose (to entertain, to invite, to inform, to wish, to remember) and explains the clues.
  4. Read Noah's invitation and answer: Quand? Où? Qu'est-ce qu'il y a?

Lire · Reading — Lesson 5 · Unit 5 · L'hiver

Les petits mots dans les grands mots et les affiches d'hiver

Word surgery and winter posters

C1.4C1.5C2.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Look at this word: bonhomme (snowman). Now look closer. Hidden inside it are two smaller words: bon (good) + homme (man). A snowman is a “good man”!

Puzzle: how many big words are secretly made of smaller words? If you learn to spot the little words, could you read big words you've never seen before?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C1.4Find small words inside bigger words to figure out new vocabulary (bonhomme = bon + homme).
  • C1.5Give my opinion about a poster or ad and how it's made, and point to evidence in it (colours, pictures, words).
  • C2.2Name some features of a poster (big title, picture, date, few words) and explain how they help the message.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Two skills this week

1. Word surgery. Many French words are compounds or contain familiar words. Finding them gives your child a key to decoding and meaning.

2. Media literacy. A poster is a media text designed to catch attention fast. Your child learns to notice how (big letters, bright colours, exclamation marks) and to give an opinion backed by evidence (“I like it because the snowman is big and funny”).

You can say“Let's be word surgeons! Grab your scalpel (a pencil) and find the tiny words hiding inside this big word.”
PhonicsSound of the week: an / en — both make the same nasal “ah” sound: maman, enfant, dent. Two spellings, one sound!
How you'll know it clickedYour child finds small words inside at least 5 bigger words, reads the Carnaval poster, and gives an opinion with one piece of evidence from the poster.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Do word surgery on compound words and design a better winter poster.

Materials

  • Scissors, paper strips
  • Markers, big paper
  • Examples of real posters or flyers from your community (optional)

Steps

  1. Write 6 compound words on paper strips. Child cuts them into their small words and reads each piece.
  2. Mix the pieces and re-build the words — or build silly new ones!
  3. Read the carnival poster together. Child finds each feature from Part 3 and points to it.
  4. Opinion: child rates the poster (1–5 snowflakes) and gives a reason with evidence.
  5. Design a better poster for your own winter event: big title, picture, date, place and one exciting sentence.

Record your observations

Big wordSmall wordsMeaning

Assignment · Le devoir

Notebook work.

Part A — Word surgery page

Draw 4 compound words as funny pictures (e.g., a bald mouse for chauve-souris). Label the parts.

Part B — Poster review

Draw the carnival poster from memory. Write (dictate) what you like and what you'd change, with a reason.

Part C — an / en hunt

Find 6 words with an or en in this lesson. Copy them and circle the sound.

Homework · À la maison

1 · Poster hunt

Find a real poster or flyer (at the library, grocery store, school). What features does it use? Is it good? Why?

2 · Hidden words

In any book or sign, look for small words hidden in big words (in French or English: “snowman”, “butterfly”!).

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Why does a butterfly have “butter” in its name? Who decides what things are called?
  2. Posters try to make us do things. Is that good or bad? Can a poster ever trick you?
  3. Could a language be made of only short words? What would long ideas look like?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Lire · Reading — Lesson 6 · Unit 6 · Miam!

Les menus, les recettes et les emballages

Menus, recipes and bilingual boxes

C1.2C1.5C2.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Pick up almost any cereal box, juice carton or granola bar wrapper in Canada. Look carefully. You'll find French on it — every single time.

Puzzle: why would a company print everything twice, in two languages? Who decided that? And when the French and English on the same box say slightly different things… which one is telling the truth?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C1.2Read and understand a menu and a simple recipe with familiar food words and pictures.
  • C2.1Explain the purpose of a menu (to choose), a recipe (to follow steps) and a food package (to inform and to sell).
  • C1.5Give my opinion about a food package's message and design, with evidence (pictures, colours, words).

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Real-world reading

This week uses real texts from your kitchen. Canada's Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act requires most packaged food to be labelled in both English and French — so your pantry is a French reading library! Gather 4–5 boxes before starting.

Sound of the week: é

The letter é (with its accent aigu) always says “ay”. So do the endings -er and -ez at the end of many words: manger, mangez.

You can say“Look! This box speaks two languages, just like you're learning to. Let's find the French side and read it like detectives.”
Cook togetherRecipes are a great way to read with purpose: the child reads each step and you do it together. Following written instructions is a key reading skill across all subjects.
How you'll know it clickedYour child reads the menu and orders from it, follows the 4-step recipe by reading each step aloud, and explains what a package is trying to make them do or believe.

The Lesson · La leçon

Le son de la semaine · Sound of the week: é (-er, -ez)

é always says “ay”. The endings -er and -ez usually say “ay” too.

bébébay-BAYbabycaféka-FAYcoffeeépicerieay-pee-SREEgrocerymangerma(n)-ZHAYto eatmélangermay-la(n)-ZHAYto mixfermezfehr-MAYclose (plural)

Mots fréquents · Sight words (learn to read these by sight)

aimeehmlikene … pasnuh … panotdudüsomeauohat the / withmaismehbutouooor
Part 1 · Le menu du Café Léa
Surprising factIn Canada, French speakers call breakfast le déjeuner, lunch le dîner and supper le souper. In France, breakfast is le petit-déjeuner, lunch is le déjeuner and dinner is le dîner! So if a Canadian and a French person agree to meet for le dîner, one arrives at noon and the other at 7 p.m.!
Part 2 · Une recette: la salade de fruits

A recipe is a text you follow. Its steps are numbered and in order. Read each step, then do it!

Part 3 · Read a box — two languages

Find a cereal box or juice carton. Look for these French words — they're on almost every package in Canada:

French on the boxEnglish on the boxWhy it's there
Ingrédientsa(n)-gray-DYA(N)IngredientsIngredientsTo tell you what's inside
Valeur nutritiveva-LUHR nü-tree-TEEVNutrition factsNutrition FactsHealth information
Nouveau!noo-VOHNew!New!To make you want it
Sans arachidessa(n) za-ra-SHEEDPeanut-freePeanut-freeSafety
Délicieux!day-lee-SYUHDelicious!Delicious!To convince you
Part 4 · Media detective: what is the box trying to do?

A food box has two jobs: to inform (what's inside) and to sell (make you want it). Look at your box. Which parts inform? Which parts sell? Is there a cartoon character? Bright colours? A toy? Why?

Je pense que…zhuh pa(n)s kuhI think that…La boîte veut que j'achète…la bwat vuh kuh zha-SHEHTThe box wants me to buy…C'est vrai. / Ce n'est pas vrai.seh VREH / suh neh pa VREHIt's true. / It's not true.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
On Café Léa's menu, what would you choose for le dîner? How much does it cost?
Stretch
Why are the recipe steps numbered? What would happen if you did step 4 before step 1?
Challenge
A cereal box says Délicieux! Is that information or selling? How could you find out if it's true?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Read and follow a French recipe, and compare French and English on real packages.

Materials

  • Fruit salad ingredients and a bowl
  • 4–5 bilingual food packages
  • Highlighters (two colours)

Steps

  1. Read the ingredient list aloud and gather each item — say its French name.
  2. Make the fruit salad: child reads each step aloud before you do it together.
  3. Package reading: find the French side of each box. Highlight French words you can read in one colour, and cognates in another.
  4. Sort the words on each box: inform or sell?
  5. Open Café Léa: child reads the menu and takes your order; you pay in pretend money.

PackageFrench words I readInform or sell?My opinion

Assignment · Le devoir

Notebook work.

Part A — My menu

Make your own café menu with 4 foods and prices. Copy the headings Le déjeuner, Le dîner, Les desserts.

Part B — Recipe order

Parent writes the 4 recipe steps on strips, mixed up. Child reads and puts them in order, then glues them in.

Part C — Box report

Draw the front of a real food box. Label 2 French words. Answer: What is this box trying to make me do? Do I believe it? Why?

Homework · À la maison

1 · Pantry reading

Read one French word from a different package every day. Keep a list on the fridge.

2 · Cook from French

Cook one more simple recipe together from the French instructions (a sandwich, a smoothie). Child reads, you cook.

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. If a box said something that wasn't true, who should check? Who protects us from false messages?
  2. Why do you think Canada chose to have two official languages?
  3. If you designed a cereal, what would your box say to make kids want it — honestly?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Lire · Reading — Lesson 7 · Unit 7 · Les animaux

Les livres documentaires sur les animaux

Animal fact books: reading to learn

C1.1C1.3C2.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

A storybook and a fact book can both be about a bear. But one might have a bear who talks and wears a hat, and the other tells you a bear's heart slows down to 8 beats a minute when it hibernates.

Puzzle: how do you know, before you start reading, whether a book is going to tell you a story or tell you the truth? What clues on the page give it away?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C2.2Identify features of an information text — title, photos, captions, labels, headings, fact boxes — and explain how they help me learn.
  • C1.1Use reading strategies for information texts: look at headings and pictures first, ask questions, then read to find answers.
  • C1.3Read short information sentences about animals smoothly and with understanding.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Fiction vs non-fiction

This is your child's first non-fiction reading. The strategy: Preview (look at the title, photos and headings), Question (What do I want to find out?), Read (find the answers), Tell (say what I learned). You can call it “P-Q-R-T” or draw 4 icons.

Sound of the week: oi

o + i = “wa”: moi, trois, oiseau, poisson. Children find this one funny!

You can say“Before we read a fact book, we take a tour. Let's look at the title, the pictures and the little captions. What do you think we'll learn?”
LibraryBorrow a French non-fiction animal book from the library if you can (ask for “documentaires pour enfants”). Even if the text is too hard, your child can use the features — photos, labels, captions — to learn.
How you'll know it clickedYour child can point to and name at least 4 features of an information text, explain what each one is for, read the ours noir fact page, and answer 3 questions about it.

The Lesson · La leçon

o + i = “wa” — a surprising sound!

Feature (French)What it isWhat it does for me

Part 2 · Fact page: L'ours noir

Preview: Read the title and headings (the bold words) first. Question: What do you want to know about black bears? Read. Tell.

Surprising factBlack bears aren't always black! In parts of Canada, some are brown, cinnamon, and a rare kind in British Columbia is white: the Kermode bear or “spirit bear”, sacred to the Kitasoo/Xai'xais and Gitga'at First Nations.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Which feature helped you most on the black bear page: the headings, the photo (in your mind), or the Le sais-tu? box? Why?
Stretch
You want to know only what black bears eat. Do you need to read the whole page? How would you find it fast?
Challenge
“La petite cabane dans la forêt” (Lesson A7) had a bear in it too. Is it fiction or non-fiction? Find 3 clues to prove it.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Create a mini fact book with real information text features.

Materials

  • 3 sheets folded into a 6-page booklet
  • Crayons, pencils
  • A French or English animal fact book from the library (optional)

Steps

  1. Book tour: look at a real fact book together. Find and name each feature from Part 1.
  2. Choose a Canadian animal (castor, orignal, loup, renard, hibou…).
  3. Plan pages: 1 = title page, 2 = table of contents, 3 = Son corps (labelled diagram), 4 = Où il vit, 5 = Ce qu'il mange, 6 = Le sais-tu? fact box.
  4. Write one sentence per page (copy frames from Part 2, change the details), add drawings, labels and one caption.
  5. Read your fact book to the family and let them ask questions.

PageFeature I usedMy sentence

Notebook work.

Part A — Feature match

Parent draws 4 boxes: title, photo, caption, labels. Child draws an example of each and says what it's for.

Part B — Bear quiz

Answer from the fact page: Where does the black bear live? What does it eat? What happens in winter?

Part C — oi words

Copy 5 oi words. Read them fast to your parent 3 times.

Homework · À la maison

1 · Library fact book

Borrow one fact book about an animal. Find 4 features. What did you learn?

2 · Label the house pet or a toy

Draw a pet or stuffed animal and label its body parts in French.

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. How do scientists find out facts about animals that live deep in the sea or sleep all winter?
  2. Can a story teach you true things too? Can a fact book ever be wrong?
  3. If someone made a fact book about you, what would be in the Le sais-tu? box?

Lire · Reading — Lesson 8 · Unit 8 · Le calendrier et la météo

Je lis le calendrier et je me connais comme lecteur

Reading the calendar and knowing myself as a reader

C1.3C1.4C2.3
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

You can “read” things that aren't sentences: a calendar, a clock, a weather map, a bus schedule. Each one is a kind of code.

Puzzle: is reading a calendar the same skill as reading a story? What does your brain do differently? And after almost a whole year… what kind of reader have you become?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C1.3Read a calendar, a weather diary and a short seasons text smoothly, with understanding.
  • C1.4Use vocabulary strategies: word families (pluie, pleut, parapluie), known words and pictures.
  • C2.3(a) Name reading strategies that help me; (b) know my strengths and next steps as a reader.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Metacognition for readers

This week combines calendar/season reading with a reflection on your child as a reader. Before the reflection, look back at the texts from Unit 1: can your child read them easily now? That comparison is powerful evidence of growth.

Sound of the week: ai / è / ê

ai, è, ê (and often et at the end of words) all say “eh”: lait, mère, fête, jouet.

You can say“Look how far you've come! In September you were reading letters. Now you read whole pages. Let's figure out what helped you the most.”
How you'll know it clickedYour child reads the calendar page and answers 4 questions about it, finds 3 word-family members, and names two reading strategies and one reading goal.

The Lesson · La leçon

Le son de la semaine · Sound of the week: ai / è / ê

ai, è and ê all say “eh”, like in “bed”.

Part 1 · Le calendrier d'avril
Surprising factIn France and Quebec, April Fool's Day is called Poisson d'avril — “April fish”! Children secretly stick a paper fish on someone's back and then shout “Poisson d'avril!” Nobody is completely sure how it started — one idea is that April 1st was near the end of the fishing season.
Part 2 · Word families

Words in the same family share a piece. If you know one, you can guess the others!

FamilyMembersWhat they share
pluie (rain)la pluiela PLWEEthe rain il pleuteel PLUHit's raining le parapluieluh pa-ra-PLWEEthe umbrella pluvieuxplü-VYUHrainyrain
neige (snow)la neigela NEHZHthe snow il neigeeel NEHZHit's snowing le bonhomme de neigeluh bo-NUM duh NEHZHthe snowman enneigéa(n)-neh-ZHAYsnowysnow
soleil (sun)le soleilluh so-LEYthe sun ensoleilléa(n)-so-ley-YAYsunny le tournesolluh toor-nuh-SOLthe sunflowersun (sol)

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Tournesol (sunflower) means “turns to the sun”! Young sunflowers really do turn their heads to follow the sun across the sky during the day. Scientists call this heliotropism.
Part 3 · Les saisons — a reading page
Part 4 · Me as a reader

Which of these reading strategies do you use? Tick them in your head, then say them to your parent.

  • I look at the pictures first.
  • I point to each word.
  • I sound out the letters and letter teams (ou, on, ch, oi…).
  • I look for words I know and mots amis.
  • I look for small words inside big words.
  • I make a movie in my mind.
  • I re-read when it doesn't make sense.
  • I ask what a word means.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
On the calendar, which day of the week is Earth Day? What will the class do on April 24th if it rains?
Stretch
You meet a new word: neigeux. Which family does it belong to? What might it mean?
Challenge
Is reading a calendar the same as reading a story? What's different about how your eyes move and what your brain looks for?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Build a word-family tree and do a “then and now” reading check.

Materials

  • Big paper with a tree drawn on it
  • Leaf-shaped sticky notes or paper leaves
  • The Unit 1 texts (Lesson C1)
  • Timer

Steps

  1. Word-family trees: draw 4 trees (pluie, neige, soleil, jour). Child reads each family word and sticks it as a leaf on the right tree.
  2. Read the calendar: parent asks questions (Quand est l'anniversaire de Noah?); child finds the answer.
  3. Then and now: child reads the Lesson C1 name cards and greeting cards. How easy is it now? Time it.
  4. Read Les quatre saisons twice. Mark 3 words that were hard.
  5. Fill in the reader reflection table.

Record your observations

TextEasy / OK / hardStrategy I used

Part A — My calendar

Make a calendar page for next month. Copy the month name and the days. Add 3 events in French (a birthday, a holiday, a special day).

Part B — Reader self-portrait

Draw yourself reading. Around you, write (dictate) your 3 best reading strategies.

Part C — Strengths and next steps

DayWhat I readMinutes

  2. Do you read differently when you read for fun and when you read for information?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Lire · Reading — Lesson 9 · Unit 9 · Ma communauté, notre francophonie

Je lis ma communauté: affiches, cartes postales et lettres

Reading my francophone community: signs, postcards and letters

C3.1C3.2C1.5C2.3
1–2 weeks · 5–8 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Look at a red octagon-shaped stop sign in Ottawa. It might say STOP, ARRÊT — or both. In Quebec, it says only ARRÊT. In France, it says STOP!

Puzzle: France is where French began — so why does a French stop sign use an English word, while Quebec uses a French one? What can signs tell us about the people who live in a place?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • C3.1Read texts about francophone communities in Ontario and around the world, and connect them to my community and my life.
  • C3.2Find polite and friendly conventions in written French: Cher / Chère, Bonjour, Salut, Amicalement, Bisous, and tu / vous in letters and signs.
  • C1.5Give my opinion about community signs and a tourism message, with evidence from the text.
  • C2.3Look back at my year as a reader: my favourite texts, strategies, strengths and goals.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Final reading lesson

Your child reads community texts (signs, postcards, a letter) and learns about francophone places. It pairs perfectly with a real outing: many Ontario communities have bilingual signs, and some have French-only ones.

Sound of the week: in / ain / un

All three make the same nasal sound, like the “a” in “bag” through the nose: lapin, main, un. Also gn = “ny”: montagne.

You can say“Signs, postcards and letters show us how people live and talk to each other. Let's read our community like a book!”
How you'll know it clickedYour child reads 5 community signs, reads both postcards and says who each one is written to (friend or adult) and how they know, and completes the year-end reading reflection.

The Lesson · La leçon

Le son de la semaine · Sound of the week: in / ain / un · gn

in, ain, un make one nasal sound. gn sounds like “ny” in canyon.
