Surprising factTirez means pull — but it looks like it might mean something else to English speakers. Many English-speaking tourists in France and Quebec push doors marked Tirez! Now you won't.
Part 2 · Two postcards — who are they for?

Which postcard is to a friend? Which is to a teacher? Look for the clues: Salut / Chère Madame, Bisous / Amicalement, and in card 2, Léa writes vous (polite) to her teacher.

Surprising factNew Brunswick is Canada's only officially bilingual province. The Acadians, French-speaking people who have lived in the Maritimes since the 1600s, celebrate their national day on August 15 with the Tintamarre — a noisy parade where everyone makes as much noise as possible with pots, pans and horns!
Part 3 · A tourism message

Media detective: What does this message want you to do? Which words make Sudbury sound exciting (géante, magnifiques, découvrir)? Would you like to go? Why? Is anything left out?

Part 4 · My year of reading

Look back at all the texts you read this year: name cards, labels, pattern books, family books, invitations, posters, menus, recipes, fact pages, calendars, postcards. Wow!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
What's the difference between Bisous and Amicalement? When would you use each one?
Stretch
The tourism message only says good things about Sudbury. Why? Is it lying, or just choosing?
Challenge
Why do you think some towns in Ontario have signs in both languages and some only in English? Who might decide? (Parent: Ontario's French Language Services Act designates areas where provincial services are offered in French.)

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Go on a community sign walk and write back to a postcard.

Materials

  • Phone/camera
  • Clipboard and paper
  • A blank postcard or index card

Steps

  1. Sign walk: walk around your neighbourhood, a mall or a government building. Photograph or note any French signs. (Ontario government buildings, Canada Post, and highways often have French.)
  2. Read each sign aloud. What does it mean? Who is it for?
  3. Read both postcards again. Sort the clue words: friendly vs polite.
  4. Write back to Léa's postcard 1 as Noah (friendly), or to postcard 2 as Madame Diallo — choose the right greeting and closing!
  5. Discuss the Sudbury message: rate it and give evidence.

Make a mini-book of 5 French signs (drawn or photographed) with their meanings.

  2. Why do people send postcards when they can send a text message instantly?

Écrire

Writing is where everything comes together. Grade 1 writers learn by copying and changing models, building a personal dictionary, and following the real writing process — plan, draft, revise, edit, publish — to make cards, books, posters, menus, journals and letters for real readers. All 11 writing expectations (D1.1–D3.2) are covered.

Lessons · Leçons

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 1 · Unit 1 · Bonjour!

J'écris mon nom et une carte

My name, my card: writing to someone

D1.1D1.2D3.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Before anyone could phone or text, people sent letters and cards that took weeks to arrive. Some letters written more than 300 years ago still exist today — and we can still read them!

Puzzle: spoken words disappear the moment you say them. Written words can last for centuries. So who will read what you write this week — and what do you want them to feel when they read it?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.1Decide, with help, why I'm writing (purpose) and who will read it (audience) before I start.
  • D1.2Write my name and short sentences about myself (Je m'appelle… J'ai… ans.) following a model.
  • D3.2Use the right greeting and closing in a card: Salut / Bonjour / Cher, Chère and Bisous / De / À bientôt.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

How Grade 1 French writing works

At this age, children write by copying and adapting models. They are not expected to spell from memory. Every writing lesson gives your child a sentence frame (a model with a blank) to copy and complete. That's exactly how immersion teachers do it. Accept invented spelling for extra words, but insist on careful copying of the model.

Before any writing — ask two questions
  1. Pourquoi j'écris? (Why am I writing?) — to say hello, to thank, to tell, to invite…
  2. Pour qui j'écris? (Who am I writing for?) — a friend, grandma, a teacher…

Post these two questions above the writing space all year.

You can say“Before we write, we ask: Pourquoi? and Pour qui? Why are we writing, and who's going to read it? That changes the words we choose!”
HandwritingFrench handwriting: in Canadian French schools, Grade 1 children usually print (écriture script). Accents are written after the letter is finished: write the e, then add the accent on top.
Watch for this misconceptionChildren often forget accents or place them anywhere. Model: é (accent goes up to the right ↗, like a slide going up), è (goes down to the right ↘). A fun rule: é = “ay” = smile up!
How you'll know it clickedYour child writes their name and 2 model sentences independently, answers Pourquoi? Pour qui? before writing, and chooses Salut or Bonjour/Cher correctly for the reader of their card.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Writing my name

Your name is the most important word you'll ever write! Write it with a capital letter (majuscule) at the start. In French, names always start with a capital: Léa, Noah, Samuel.

Modèle: Je me présente · Model: introducing myself
  1. My name is ___.
  2. I am ___ years old.
  3. I am happy. (boy / girl)
  4. I like ___.

Part 3 · Cher or chère?

Cher means “dear”. Write Cher for a boy or man, and Chère (with an extra e and an accent) for a girl or woman. They sound exactly the same!

Cher papa,SHEHR pa-PADear Dad,Chère maman,SHEHR ma-MA(N)Dear Mom,Cher Noah,SHEHR no-ADear Noah,Chère Madame Diallo,SHEHR ma-DAM dya-LOHDear Madame Diallo,
Part 4 · A model card
Surprising factFrench uses different quotation marks from English. Instead of “these”, French writes « these » — they're called guillemets, named after a printer called Guillaume (William) who may have invented them about 500 years ago!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Léa wrote Bisous to grandma. Would she write Bisous to her teacher? Why not?
Stretch
Why do you think French has two spellings (Cher / Chère) that sound the same? Who can tell the difference — someone listening, or someone reading?
Challenge
Written words can last hundreds of years. If you wrote a card that someone read in 100 years, what would you want to tell them about you?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Plan and write a real card with the right greeting, closing and sentences about yourself.

Materials

  • Card stock or folded paper
  • Pencil, crayons, stickers
  • An envelope (optional)

Steps

  1. Choose a real reader (grandparent, friend, neighbour). Answer Pourquoi? Pour qui? and write it on a sticky note.
  2. Choose the greeting (Salut / Bonjour / Cher / Chère) and closing (Bisous / De / À bientôt) that fit that reader.
  3. Copy the model sentences from Part 1 and complete the blanks with your information.
  4. Decorate the card. Read it aloud to check.
  5. Deliver or mail it! (Publishing = giving your writing to a real reader.)

Notebook work — the first page of Mon cahier de français.

Part A — My title page

Write Mon cahier de français and your name in your best printing. Draw yourself.

Part B — About me

Copy and complete the 4 model sentences. Draw a picture for each.

Part C — Greetings sort

Parent writes 6 words on cards: Salut, Bonjour, Cher, Bisous, De, Chère Madame. Child sorts them into “for friends/family” and “for adults I respect”, then copies them in two columns.

Homework · À la maison

1 · Name everywhere

This week, your child writes their name on everything they create — drawings, lunch notes, a door sign La chambre de ___.

2 · A second card

Write a card to a different kind of reader (if the first was to family, now to an adult you respect). Change the greeting and closing!

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Why do you think people started writing things down? What was the first thing someone ever needed to remember?
  2. Is a text message a kind of letter? What's different?
  3. If you could write a letter to anyone in the world — alive or from history — who would it be and what would you say?

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 2 · Unit 2 · Mon école

Mon dictionnaire personnel et mes listes

My personal dictionary and lists

D1.3D2.1D1.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

The biggest French dictionary has more than 100,000 words. Nobody knows them all — not even the people who write dictionaries!

Puzzle: if nobody knows every word, how do writers find the words they need? What if you made a dictionary with only your words — the words you need most? What would go in it first?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.3Start and use a personal word list (Mon dictionnaire) to find and check words when I write.
  • D2.1Brainstorm ideas and words before writing (word webs, lists, pictures).
  • D1.2Write lists and labels about my school and classroom (Ma liste de fournitures: un crayon, une gomme…).

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The personal dictionary — your child's most important writing tool

Take a small notebook (or staple paper). Give each letter A–Z its own page. Every time your child learns a word they want to write, they add it on the right letter page with a small drawing. By June it will be full. From now on, when your child asks “How do you write…?”, answer: “Let's check your dictionary!” If it's not there, write it together and add it.

Brainstorming

Before writing, always brainstorm. A word web (une toile de mots): write the topic in a circle, draw lines outward, add a word and picture at the end of each line.

You can say“Writers don't keep every word in their heads. They use tools! Your dictionary is your writing tool. Let's fill it with your most important words.”
Dictionary tipWrite un or une in front of every noun in the dictionary: une gomme, un crayon. That way your child always has the right little word.
How you'll know it clickedYour child's dictionary has at least 20 words with pictures; they look up a word there without prompting while writing; they produce a word web and a list of 6+ items.

Part 3 · Writing a list

A list is a text for remembering. Lists don't need full sentences — just one item per line, often with a number or a dash.

Surprising factThe Académie française in Paris has been working on its official French dictionary since 1635. It's still not finished updating it! Its members are called les Immortels (the Immortals). Haitian-Canadian writer Dany Laferrière became one of them in 2013 — the first Canadian and the first Haitian ever elected.

  2. It's my ___. (girl-word)
  3. Here are my ___. (plural)

Warm-up

Stretch

Challenge
If you had to make a dictionary for an alien learning about Earth, what would the first 5 words be? Why?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Build your personal dictionary and use it to write a list and labels.

Materials

  • A small notebook with A–Z tabs (or 26 stapled pages)
  • Coloured pencils
  • Sticky notes

Steps

  1. Make the dictionary: label each page with a letter (capital and small: Aa, Bb…).
  2. Add the Part 1 words with drawings. Say each word as you write it.
  3. Brainstorm a word web about Mon école on a big paper. Add at least 6 words.
  4. Write your own supply list (Part 3) using your dictionary to check spelling.
  5. Write 4 labels for things in your room with the Part 4 frames and stick them on.

Notebook work.

Copy your word web about Mon école into your notebook with 6 words and drawings.

Part B — My list

Write a list of 6 things for a purpose you choose: a picnic, a sleepover, a trip. Use your dictionary and add new words to it.

1 · Five new words

Add 5 new words to your dictionary this week — words YOU want to write (your favourite toy, food, animal…). Ask a parent to find them with the speaker or a French dictionary.

2 · Family list

Help write the family grocery list in French (with the dictionary). Take it to the store!

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Where do new words come from? Who invented the word “emoji” or “selfie”?
  2. Could you write a whole story using only 20 words? Try it in your head!

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 3 · Unit 3 · Mon corps

J'écris un livre à motifs: « Je peux… »

Following a pattern: writing my own pattern book

D1.4D2.2D1.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Your body can do amazing things. Your eyes can see a candle flame kilometres away on a dark night. Your hands can learn to play piano, knit, or draw. Your legs can learn to jump, swim, skate…

Puzzle: what can your body do that makes you proud? If you wrote a book called Je peux… (I can…), what would be on the most surprising page?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.4Begin to show my own voice by using a familiar pattern to write a book about me (Avec mes mains, je peux…).
  • D2.2Plan and draft with words and pictures following a model, then revise to make it more interesting (add a colour, a number, a feeling).
  • D1.2Write several sentences about myself and my body following a model.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The writing process begins

This is your child's first “book”. You'll introduce the stages of the writing process: plan (brainstorm pictures), draft (first copy — messy is OK), revise (make it better: add a detail), publish (neat copy, cover, read to someone). Make a poster of these four steps with icons.

Voice

“Voice” means the writing sounds like your child. Encourage personal, surprising pages: “With my feet I can… dance like a penguin!” Help with the French for their idea, but the idea must be theirs.

You can say“A pattern is like a train track. Every page runs on the same track — Avec mes…, je peux… — but you choose where the train goes!”
Grammar in a sentenceJe peux (I can) + an action word ending in -er, -ir, -re (these are verbs in their “name form”, the infinitive): Je peux sauter, courir, écrire. Children love this frame because it works with almost any action.
How you'll know it clickedYour child writes a 6-page pattern book with the frame, at least one page they revised to add a detail, and at least one page that shows their personal voice (a funny or surprising idea).

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · The pattern
Modèle: Je peux… · Model: I can…
  1. With my eyes, I can see ___.
  2. With my ears, I can hear ___.
  3. With my nose, I can smell ___.
  4. With my mouth, I can eat ___.
  5. With my hands, I can ___.
  6. With my feet, I can ___.

Surprising factYour nose can tell apart at least one trillion different smells, according to a 2014 study — far more than the number of colours your eyes can see! Babies can recognise their mother by smell within days of being born.

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
What did Léa add to make her pages better? Which revision do you like most? Why?
Stretch
What makes a page sound like you and not like everyone else? Give an example.
Challenge
Invent a new pattern for a book about your body: Quand je suis content, mon corps… (When I'm happy, my body…). Write the first page.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Plan, draft, revise and publish a 6-page pattern book.

Materials

  • Scrap paper for the draft
  • 3 sheets folded and stapled for the final book
  • Crayons, pencil, eraser

Steps

  1. Plan: for each body part, draw a quick sketch of what you can do.
  2. Draft: on scrap paper, copy the frame and fill in the blank for each page.
  3. Revise: choose 2 pages and add a detail (colour, number, comme un… comparison).
  4. Edit: check capitals and periods with the checklist.
  5. Publish: copy neatly into the booklet, add a cover (Je peux! par ___) and illustrations. Read it to the family!

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 4 · Unit 4 · Ma famille, ma maison

Ma famille et une carte de fêtes: je corrige mon texte

My family page and a holiday card: editing like a pro

D1.2D2.3D3.2
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Professional writers — the people who write the books in the library — almost never get it right the first time. Many of them rewrite a page five, ten or twenty times. Then an editor reads it and finds even more to fix!

Puzzle: if even professionals make mistakes, what's the secret to writing that looks perfect? Could you become your own editor?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.2Write several sentences about my family and home following a model (Dans ma famille, il y a… Voici…).
  • D2.3Edit and proofread with a checklist (capitals, periods, spaces, copying carefully), then publish a neat copy.
  • D3.2Use holiday and card conventions correctly: Joyeuses fêtes! Bonne année! Cher/Chère… Avec amour…

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Editing, for real

This week introduces the editing checklist (ma liste de vérification), which your child will use for every piece of writing from now on. Keep it simple: 5 checks. Print or copy it into the back of the notebook.

The holiday card

December is perfect for writing cards. Choose the greeting that fits your family's traditions — many are listed in Part 3 (Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa, Diwali (earlier in fall), New Year, or the neutral Joyeuses fêtes).

You can say“Now you're the editor! Grab your editor's pencil (a coloured pencil). Let's check one thing at a time.”
Editing tipLet your child find the mistakes. Say “I see 2 missing periods on this page — can you find them?” instead of pointing directly. Finding errors is the skill.
How you'll know it clickedYour child writes a 4–5 sentence family page, uses the checklist to find and fix at least 2 errors in their own draft, and writes a holiday card with a correct greeting and closing.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · My family page — the model
Modèle: Ma famille · Model: My family
  1. In my family, there are ___ people.
  2. There's my mom, my dad and ___.
  3. My brother / sister is called ___.
  4. I live in a house / an apartment.
  5. My favourite room is ___.
  6. I love my family!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Why do names like Samuel and Ottawa need a capital letter? What would happen if we didn't use capitals?
Stretch

Challenge

Objective: Write, edit and publish a family page and a holiday card.

Materials

  • Good paper (final copy)

Steps

  2. Edit with the checklist, one check at a time, using the coloured pencil to fix mistakes.
  3. Publish: copy neatly onto good paper. Add it to your portfolio.

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 5 · Unit 5 · L'hiver

Je crée une affiche pour le carnaval d'hiver

Make a poster! Writing a media text

D1.5D1.1D2.1
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

A poster has about 3 seconds to catch someone's attention as they walk by. Three seconds! That's less time than it takes to say your full name and address.

Puzzle: if you only had 3 seconds to convince someone to come to your winter party, what would you put on your poster? What would you leave out?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.5Create a media text (a poster) in French using simple conventions: big title, picture, key information, an exciting phrase.
  • D1.1Decide the purpose (to invite, to inform, to convince) and the audience of my poster before I design it.
  • D2.1Generate and organise ideas with a brainstorm and a plan (sketch) before making the final poster.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Media writing

This lesson connects Reading C5 (reading a poster) with writing one. Your child will plan a real or pretend winter event — a family snow day, a hot chocolate party, a skating afternoon — and make a poster to invite people. Real events are more motivating: plan one!

Steps
  1. Look again at the carnival poster in Lesson C5.
  2. Choose the event and answer Pourquoi? Pour qui?
  3. Brainstorm: what, when, where, what fun things.
  4. Sketch (small draft), then make the big final poster.
You can say“A poster is like a shout on paper! Big words, a big picture, and only the most important information.”
Form mattersPosters don't need full sentences. Short phrases are better: Chocolat chaud gratuit! This makes writing easier and teaches that different forms have different rules.
How you'll know it clickedYour child plans and makes a poster with a big title, a date, a place, a picture and one exciting phrase — all in French — and can explain who it's for and why they made each choice.

Part 2 · Fun winter activities
des glissadesday glee-SADslides / sleddingdu patindü pa-TA(N)skatingun concours de bonhommes de neigeuh(n) ko(n)-KOOR duh bo-NUM duh NEHZHa snowman contestdu chocolat chauddü sho-ko-la SHOHhot chocolatede la tire sur la neigeduh la TEER sür la NEHZHmaple taffy on snowde la musiqueduh la mü-ZEEKmusicune bataille de boules de neigeün ba-TYE duh bool duh NEHZHa snowball fightun feu de campuh(n) fuh duh KA(N)a campfire
Part 3 · Brainstorm & plan

Before the big poster, make a small sketch (une esquisse) on scrap paper. Decide where the title, picture and information go. Designers always sketch first!

Surprising factMany famous posters were designed by artists. In Paris in the 1890s, artist Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec made posters so beautiful that people stole them off the walls at night to take home! Today they hang in museums.
Part 4 · Poster conventions
  • BIG letters for the title (capital letters are OK on posters!).
  • Bright colours that contrast (dark on light).
  • One big picture.
  • Only the most important words.
  • ! to show excitement.

Remember: in French, days and months don't take a capital letter — le samedi 23 janvier, not “Samedi 23 Janvier” (except in an all-capitals title).

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Who is your poster for? Where will you put it so they see it?
Stretch
Why do posters use short phrases instead of full sentences? Would a poster with 50 words work? Why not?
Challenge
How could you make your poster work for someone who can't read French yet? (Hint: pictures, symbols, numbers.)

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Plan and create an event poster in French.

Materials

  • Scrap paper for the sketch
  • Big paper or bristol board
  • Markers, crayons, stickers, cotton balls (snow!)
  • The C5 carnival poster for reference

Steps

  1. Decide the event, the audience and the purpose. Write them in the planning table.
  2. Brainstorm activities with the Part 2 word bank.
  3. Sketch the layout on scrap paper. Show it to a family member: can they understand it in 3 seconds?
  4. Make the final poster. Check: title, when, where, what, exciting phrase, picture.
  5. Hang it where your audience will see it. If it's a real event — hold it!

Pour qui?Pourquoi?Quand?Où?

Notebook work.

Part A — Poster plan

Glue in your sketch. Label each part: le titre, la date, le lieu (place), l'image.

Part B — The 3-second test

Show your poster to 3 people for 3 seconds. What did they remember? Write their answers. Was it what you wanted?

Part C — My choices

Explain: Why did I choose these colours, this picture, and this exciting phrase?

Homework · À la maison

1 · Poster makeover

Find a real poster or flyer. How would you make it better? Draw a small improved version.

2 · Hold the event!

If possible, hold your winter event. Did people come because of your poster?

Keep Wondering · Continue à te questionner

  1. Before posters, how did people let a whole town know about an event?
  2. Why do some posters make you want something you didn't want before? Is that a good thing?
  3. If you could make a poster that everyone in the world would see, what would it say?

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 6 · Unit 6 · Miam!

Un menu santé pour une fête de famille

A healthy menu for a family celebration

D1.1D1.2D1.3
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Every restaurant menu is a tiny piece of persuasive writing. Restaurants don't write “chicken”. They write “golden roasted chicken with fresh herbs”. Same chicken!

Puzzle: why would changing the words make food sound more delicious? Could you write a menu that makes even broccoli sound irresistible?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.1Decide my purpose and audience: a healthy menu for a real family celebration.
  • D1.2Write a menu and opinion sentences about food (J'aime… parce que c'est…).
  • D1.3Check and vary my words with my dictionary and word banks (use délicieux, croquant, sucré instead of always bon).

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Straight from the curriculum

The Ontario curriculum's own example for D1.1 is “to compile a menu of healthy foods for a class celebration”. We'll do it for a family celebration — ideally a real meal your child helps plan (a birthday, a weekend brunch, Mardi Gras/Shrove Tuesday crêpes in February).

Word choice

This is the first lesson focused on varying vocabulary. Build a “Instead of bon…” word bank together and challenge your child to never use bon on their menu.

You can say“Bon is a tired word — everyone uses it! Let's find more exciting words to make our menu delicious.”
Healthy plateCanada's Food Guide (available in French as Guide alimentaire canadien) recommends filling half your plate with vegetables and fruits, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grains. It's a great visual for the healthy menu — draw the plate!
How you'll know it clickedYour child produces a real menu with at least 3 sections, uses 3+ varied describing words, checks spelling with the dictionary, and can explain who the menu is for and why the foods are healthy.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · Instead of “bon”…

Des mots pour décrire la nourriture · Words to describe food

délicieux / délicieuseday-lee-SYUH / day-lee-SYUHZdelicioussucré / sucréesü-KRAYsweetcroquant / croquantekro-KA(N) / kro-KA(N)Tcrunchyfrais / fraîcheFREH / FREHSHfreshchaud / chaudeSHOH / SHOHDhot, warmjuteux / juteusezhü-TUH / zhü-TUHZjuicysantésa(n)-TAYhealthy (Canadian use)miam!MYAMyum!coloré / coloréeko-lo-RAYcolourfulmaisonmeh-ZO(N)homemade
Part 2 · Menu model
Part 3 · Opinion sentences — with a reason!
Modèle: mon opinion · Model: my opinion
  1. I like ___ because it's ___.
  2. I love ___ because it's ___.
  3. I don't like ___ because it's ___.
  4. ___ is good for your health!

Example: J'aime les pommes parce que c'est croquant et sucré.zhehm lay PUM par-suh-kuh seh kro-KA(N) ay sü-KRAYI like apples because they're crunchy and sweet.

Surprising factOn Mardi gras (Shrove Tuesday) and on la Chandeleur (February 2nd), French-speaking families traditionally eat crêpes. An old tradition says that if you flip a crêpe while holding a coin in your other hand and it lands perfectly in the pan, you'll have good luck all year!
Part 4 · Planning: Pourquoi? Pour qui?
QuestionExample answer
Pourquoi? (Why?)To plan a healthy meal for grandma's birthday
Pour qui? (For whom?)My whole family — 6 people, and grandma doesn't eat spicy food
Quoi? (What form?)A menu: a title, sections, food names and describing words

Warm-up
Say two sentences about the same food: one with bon and one with a more exciting word. Which one makes you hungrier?
Stretch
Your menu is for a real person. How does knowing who will eat change what you write?
Challenge
Restaurants use fancy words to sell food. Is it ever unfair? When does a describing word become a trick?

  3. Draft the menu on scrap paper: title, 3–4 sections, foods with a describing word each.
  4. Check spelling with your dictionary; add any new words to it.

  2. Does food actually taste better when it has a fancy name? How could you test it?

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 7 · Unit 7 · Les animaux

J'écris mon histoire d'animaux

My own animal story, following a model

D1.4D2.2D2.3
1–2 weeks · 5–8 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Many famous stories are built on older stories. Writers borrow a pattern — a structure — and then make it their own with new characters and a new ending. Even great authors do it!

Puzzle: if you borrowed the pattern of La petite cabane dans la forêt (Lesson A7), how could you make it so different that nobody would say you copied? What would you change first?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.4Use the pattern of a familiar story to write my own story with my own characters, setting and ending — showing my voice.
  • D2.2Plan with a story map, write a draft with words and pictures, and revise to add interest (describing words, sounds, dialogue).
  • D2.3Edit with my checklist and publish my story as a book.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

The biggest writing project so far

Your child writes a 6–8 page story using the pattern of “La petite cabane dans la forêt”: a place → one animal arrives → more animals arrive with a repeated line → a surprise ending. It can take 1–2 weeks. The finished book is a portfolio highlight.

What they change to make it theirs
  • Setting: a boat, a tent, a boot, a spaceship, a birthday cake…
  • Characters: any animals (from the A7 and B7 word banks).
  • Repeated line: their own (« Il y a de la place pour moi? » — Is there room for me?).
  • Ending: their own surprise.
You can say“You're the author now! Authors borrow shapes of stories, but they fill them with their own ideas. What will your surprise be?”
How you'll know it clickedYour child plans with a story map, writes 6+ pages following the pattern with their own setting, characters and ending, revises at least 2 pages (adding a describing word, a sound, or speech), edits with the checklist, and publishes a book.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · The story pattern
PartIn La petite cabaneIn MY story
Le débutluh day-BÜThe beginning — the settingA cabin in a snowy forestWhere? ___
Le premier personnageluh pruh-MYAY pehr-so-NAHZHThe first characterA little rabbitWho? ___
La répétitionla ray-pay-tee-SYO(N)The repetitionMore animals arrive: Je peux entrer? Oui, entre!My repeated line: ___
Le problèmeluh pro-BLEHMThe problemThe cabin gets full___
La fin surprisela fa(n) sür-PREEZThe surprise endingThe tiny owl breaks the cabin!___
Part 2 · Léa's story

What did Léa keep from the model? (The pattern: animals arrive one by one, a repeated question, a surprise.) What did she change? (The boat, the lake, the animals, the question, the sneeze ending!) That's her voice.

Part 3 · Revision tools: make it come alive
ToolExample
A describing wordun petit bateau rouge
A sound word (onomatopée)PLOUF!PLOOFSPLASH! ATCHOUM!a-CHOOMACHOO! Bzzz!bzzzBzzz! BOUM!BOOMBOOM! CRAC!KRAKCRACK!

Surprising factIn French comics (bandes dessinées), sounds are different: a sneeze is atchoum, a splash is plouf, a kiss is smack and a punch is paf or bing! Belgium and France are famous for comics: Tintin was created in Belgium in 1929 and has been translated into more than 100 languages.

☐I read my sentence out loud. Does it make sense?

Extra check for stories: Did I put the speech in « guillemets »? Does my title have a capital letter? Did I write Fin at the end?

Warm-up
What's the repeated line in Léa's story? Why do you think repeating it makes the story fun?
Stretch
Léa's ending is a sneeze. Think of 3 other surprise endings for her boat story. Which is funniest?
Challenge
When is borrowing a story pattern OK, and when would it be copying? Where's the line?

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Plan, draft, revise, edit and publish an original animal story book.

Materials

  • Scrap paper for the draft
  • 8 sheets folded into a book

Steps

  1. Plan: fill in the “In MY story” column of the story map with drawings and words.
  2. Draft: one page per story part; copy frames from the model and change the details. Draw quick sketches.
  3. Revise: add at least 2 revision tools (a sound word, a describing word, speech in « »).
  4. Edit: use the checklist on every page.
  5. Publish: neat copy, full-colour pictures, cover with title and par ___ (by ___). Hold an “author reading”!

Part B — Before and after

Copy one draft sentence and the revised version. What did you add?

Part C — Feedback

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 8 · Unit 8 · Le calendrier et la météo

Mon journal météo et moi comme écrivain

My weather journal and me as a writer

D1.2D1.5D2.4
1 week · 5 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Scientists know what the weather was like in Canada 200 years ago, even before thermometers were common. How? Because people — farmers, fur traders, nuns in Quebec — wrote about the weather in their diaries, every single day.

Puzzle: could your writing be useful to someone 200 years from now? What would you want them to know about the weather — and about you?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D1.2Write daily journal entries about the date, weather and my activities following a model.
  • D1.5Create a media text: an illustrated weather report or a class calendar for others to use.
  • D2.4(a) Describe writing strategies that help me; (b) know my strengths and next steps as a writer.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Journal writing

A daily journal (journal) is how most immersion classrooms build writing fluency: a short entry every day, same frame, growing little by little. Start this week and — ideally — keep it going until June.

Writer reflection

Collect writing from the whole year: the card from D1, the dictionary, the Je peux book, the family page, the poster, the menu, the story. Spread them out. Let your child see their growth before reflecting.

You can say“Look at all this writing! In September you wrote your name. Now you write books! What helped you grow the most?”
For you, parentHudson's Bay Company fur-trading posts kept weather journals from the 1700s, and scientists today use them to study how Canada's climate has changed. Ordinary people writing every day created a scientific treasure!
How you'll know it clickedYour child writes a journal entry of 3+ sentences independently with the frame, creates a weather report or calendar page for others, and names their writing strengths and a goal.

The Lesson · La leçon

Part 1 · The journal frame
Modèle: mon journal · Model: my journal
  1. Today is ___ (day), the ___ (date) ___ (month).
  2. It's ___. / It's raining. / It's snowing.
  3. I'm wearing ___.
  4. Today, I ___ (did something).
  5. I feel ___.

Useful past-tense phrases for “what I did”: j'ai jouézhay zhoo-AYI played j'ai mangézhay ma(n)-ZHAYI ate j'ai luzhay LÜI read je suis allé(e) au parczhuh swee-za-LAY oh PARKI went to the park j'ai dessinézhay day-see-NAYI drew j'ai vuzhay VÜI saw

Part 2 · Weather words for writing
Il fait beau.eel feh BOHIt's nice out.Il fait frais.eel feh FREHIt's cool.Il y a des nuages.eel ya day nü-AHZHThere are clouds.Il y a un orage.eel ya uh(n) no-RAHZHThere's a storm.Il y a un arc-en-ciel!eel ya uh(n) nar-ka(n)-SYELLThere's a rainbow!Il fait 12 degrés.eel feh DOOZ duh-GRAYIt's 12 degrees.
Part 3 · A media text: the weather report card

Make a weather report for your family's week — like a TV weather board. Include: days of the week, a symbol for each day, the temperature and a sentence of advice (Prenez vos parapluies!).

Did you know? · Le savais-tu?Days and months in French never get a capital letter in the middle of a sentence: lundi le 19 avril. But in English they always do: Monday, April. If you forget capitals on days in English, you're thinking in French!

Mini-games · Les jeux de la leçon

Écrire · Writing — Lesson 9 · Unit 9 · Ma communauté, notre francophonie

Une lettre de l'Ontario français: je publie

A letter from French Ontario: publishing for the world

D3.1D3.2D2.3D2.4
1–2 weeks · 5–8 sessions of 45–60 min

Wonder Hook · La grande question

Somewhere in a French school in Senegal, Haiti, Belgium or Quebec, there's a Grade 1 child who has never heard of your town.

Puzzle: if you could write them one letter, what would you tell them about your community and about French in Ontario? What would surprise them most? And how would you start and end a letter to someone you've never met?

Learning Objectives · Objectifs

  • D3.1Write about francophone communities in Ontario and my own community — places, symbols, celebrations — and connect them to my life.
  • D3.2Use letter conventions correctly: Cher / Chère ami(e), Bonjour, tu or vous, Amicalement / À bientôt / Ton ami(e).
  • D2.3Edit, proofread and publish my letter (and send it, if possible!).
  • D2.4Reflect on my year as a writer: helpful strategies, strengths, and my goals for Grade 2.

Parent Teaching Guide · Guide du parent

Final writing project

Your child writes a friendly letter (une lettre amicale) to a real or imagined French-speaking child elsewhere, describing their community and francophone Ontario. If you can, make it real: a pen pal through a French school, a cousin, a friend's child in Quebec, or a family friend abroad.

Structure of a friendly letter

Place and date (top right) → greeting → body (3–5 sentences) → closing → signature.

You can say“A letter is like a bridge between two places. Let's build a bridge from our town to a child far away!”
Tu or vous?To a child the same age, use tu — even if you've never met. To an adult you don't know, use vous.
How you'll know it clickedYour child writes a 5+ sentence letter with the correct structure, greeting and closing, including 2+ facts about francophone Ontario and their community; edits it with the checklist; and completes the year-end writer reflection.

The Lesson · La leçon

PartFrenchExample

Greetingla salutationla sa-lü-ta-SYO(N)the greetingCher ami, / Chère amie, / Bonjour!
Bodyle corps de la lettreluh KOR duh la LETRthe body of the letter3–5 sentences about me and my community
Closingla formule de politessela for-MÜL duh po-lee-TESSthe closingÀ bientôt! / Amicalement, / Ton ami(e),

Part 2 · Léa's letter
Part 3 · Frames for my letter
Modèle: ma lettre · Model: my letter
  1. I live in ___, Ontario.
  2. In my town, there is/are ___.
  3. I like going to the ___.
  4. In Ontario, people speak French and English.
  5. The Franco-Ontarian flag is green and white.
  6. And you, ___?
Surprising factThe Ottawa newspaper Le Droit was founded in 1913 to defend French-language schools during Regulation 17 — writing was a way to protect a language! Today, francophone Ontario has its own TV channel (TFO), radio stations, a French university (Université de l'Ontario français in Toronto, opened in 2021) and hundreds of French schools.

☐des espacesday-zess-PASSspaces — a finger space between words.
☐I copied the words from my model or my dictionary carefully (letters and accents: é, è, à, ç).
☐I read my sentence out loud. Does it make sense?

Letter checks: place and date at the top? Greeting with a comma? A question for your reader? Closing and signature?

Part 5 · My writing year

You started the year writing your name. Now you can write cards, lists, labels, books, menus, posters, journals, stories and letters — in French. Bravo, l'écrivain! Bravo, l'écrivaine!

Think Like a Linguist · Pense comme un·e linguiste

Warm-up
Léa asked her reader a question at the end. Why is that a good idea in a letter?
Stretch
What would a child in Senegal or Haiti find most surprising about your town? Why?
Challenge
Léa wrote Ton amie. How would she sign a letter to a boy? To her teacher? Explain the differences.

Classwork · En classe

Objective: Write, edit, publish and send a friendly letter about your francophone community.

Materials

  • Nice paper or a card (final)

Steps

  2. Brainstorm: 3 things about your town, 2 facts about francophone Ontario, 1 question for your reader.
  3. Draft the letter with the Part 3 frames.
  4. Revise (add a describing word) and edit with the checklist.
  5. Publish: neat copy + a drawing or photo. Send it or give it! Keep a copy in the portfolio.

Words written one under the other to remember them.

I write a grocery list.

l'affichela-FEESH

the poster

A big sheet with a title and picture to share a message.

My poster is colourful!

le menuluh muh-NÜ

the menu

A list of the foods you can choose from.

Here's the party menu.

l'histoirelees-TWAR

the story

A text with characters, a problem and an ending.

My story has a surprise ending.

le journalluh zhoor-NAL

the journal / diary

A notebook where you write about your days.

I write in my journal.

la lettrela LETR

the letter

A message written to someone, with a greeting and a closing.

I send a letter to my friend.

l'auteur / l'autriceloh-TUHR / loh-TREESS

the author

The person who wrote a book (man / woman).

I'm the author of this book!
